passages.s: header
passages.t: All week this radar walked the value up the stack — the watchman, the guardrail, the gate, the larder, the passport, the lingua franca, the conductor, the ear and, this weekend, the repertoire — and built a workforce of agents that pass one door, draw on knowledge you own, carry a real identity, speak an open tongue, play in time and can be heard when they err. This morning the board hits the question that comes after you have built all that: how many of these digital workers do we actually employ — and can we name a single one of them? The freshest data says most enterprises cannot. Gartner's forecast — by 2028 the average Global Fortune 500 enterprise will run more than 150,000 AI agents, up from fewer than 15 in 2025 — landed this week not as a growth story but as a governance story, reframed across the trade press (SAP, CIO) as "agent sprawl is now a board-level issue." And the tell is the counting: only ~13% of organizations believe they have the right governance in place, and…

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: For a week this radar assembled the parts of an agentic workforce — one door, owned knowledge, an identity, a shared language, a conductor, an ear, a repertoire. This morning the governing question is no longer how do I build one agent well? It is "now that every team can spin up agents faster than anyone can track them, do I even know how many I have, who owns them, and what they are allowed to touch?" The answer, across this week's board-level coverage, is uncomfortable: most enterprises are scaling the agent population far faster than they are counting or governing it.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The datable signal — the population is exploding, and it is uncounted. Gartner's forecast that the average Global Fortune 500 enterprise will run more than 150,000 AI agents by 2028 (up from fewer than 15 in 2025) was recirculated this week (SAP, CIO, Reworked) explicitly as a governance alarm, not a bragging point. The counting gap is the story: only ~13% of organizations believe they have the right agent governance in place, and per an SAP LeanIX survey, fewer than half can produce an inventory of the agents they already run. Gartner's own framing is the tell — "organizations don't intentionally create agent sprawl… it is an after-effect of successful AI adoption" — which is exactly why it creeps up on the board.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The move — the enterprise starts building the register. The vendor response this week was uniform: by mid-2026 Microsoft, AWS and Google Cloud had each shipped or expanded agent registry, identity, governance and lifecycle capabilities — a centralized "single source of truth" for every agent, sanctioned, third-party and shadow. Okta's "AI Agents at Work 2026" report (200+ executives) puts a number on the maturity gap: 91% of organizations already use AI agents, but only ~10% have a well-developed strategy for managing the non-human identities those agents carry. The market has understood the assignment — you cannot govern what you have not first counted and named.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: 1. The population — uncounted. Gartner: ~150,000+ agents per Fortune 500 enterprise by 2028 (from <15 in 2025); only ~13% adequately governed; SAP LeanIX: fewer than half can inventory their agents. The digital workforce is arriving faster than the headcount.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: 2. The register — the fix everyone is building. Microsoft, AWS and Google Cloud all shipped agent registry / lifecycle / identity tooling by mid-2026; Okta: 91% use agents, only ~10% have a mature non-human-identity strategy. The census is the control plane: name every agent, assign an owner, scope what it can touch, retire it when it is done.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: 3. The bill — the reason the board cares now. A three-way squeeze (SAP): the workforce wants more agent permissions, the CFO says token spend is too high, the CEO wants results; Google Cloud's ROI report: 74% of production deployers report first-year ROI, but ~22% of deployments show negative ROI at 12 months and only ~12% of CEOs report both revenue gain and cost reduction. Uncounted agents are an uncounted cost — and an uncounted liability.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: Bottom line: the week built the workforce; this morning the board must count it. When an enterprise is heading toward 150,000 agents it cannot yet inventory, "we're scaling agents fast" is not a strategy — it is an unmeasured liability, because you cannot govern, budget for, audit, or stand behind a workforce you have never counted. The firm that answers "how many agents do we run?" with a shrug is running a city with no census — no way to tax, govern, or account for its residents. The firm that answers with a register — every agent named, owned, scoped and retirable — can let the population grow because it can still see it. Count before you scale: take the census, build the register, and make "we know exactly how many agents we run, who owns each, and what it can touch" the answer the board can give — because the sprawl is coming whether or not you are counting.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Census"
passages.t: Topic: This week the enterprise-AI conversation pivoted from building agents to governing the sheer number of them. Gartner's forecast that the average Global Fortune 500 enterprise will run more than 150,000 AI agents by 2028 (up from fewer than 15 in 2025) was recirculated across the trade press (SAP News, CIO, Reworked) as the framing "AI agent sprawl is now a board-level issue." The alarm is a counting gap: only about 13% of organizations believe they have the right agent governance in place, and per an SAP LeanIX survey fewer than half can even produce an inventory of the agents they already run. In response, Microsoft, AWS and Google Cloud have each shipped agent registry, identity and lifecycle tooling; Okta's "AI Agents at Work 2026" report finds 91% of organizations using agents but only ~10% with a mature strategy for the non-human identities they carry. This follows the week's editions on the gate, the larder, the passport, the lingua franca, the conductor, the ear and…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Census"
passages.t: There was a city that fell in love with hiring. Its workers were tireless — they never slept, never tired, and could be conjured by any household that wanted one — and so, quarter by quarter, every household hired more. The mayor was proud of it. "We are the fastest-growing city in the province," he told the council, and the council nodded, because everywhere you looked there was work being done: messages carried, ledgers kept, bargains struck, goods moved through the night.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Census"
passages.t: But one autumn the treasurer came to the council with a simple, terrible admission. Asked how many workers the city now employed, she could not say. Not roughly. Each household had hired on its own — through the front gate, through the back, through a cousin who knew a cousin — and no one had ever kept a roll. There was no register of who worked where, who had hired them, which doors their keys opened, or which of them were still needed and which had finished their task months ago and simply kept drawing breath and pay. The city had a hundred thousand workers and could not name one of them. It had grown too fast to count itself.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Census"
passages.t: And here the danger stopped being abstract. A worker no one remembered hiring still held a key to the treasury. A task finished in spring still had three workers assigned to it in autumn, quietly costing wages no one had budgeted. When something went wrong — a message misdelivered, a ledger altered, a door left open — no one could say which worker had done it, or who was answerable, because no one owned the roll. The city was not badly run; it was uncounted, and an uncounted city cannot be governed, cannot be taxed honestly, and cannot answer for itself when a magistrate asks who did this.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Census"
passages.t: The households that panicked did the loud thing: they froze all hiring, and watched the work stop. But the households that kept their footing did the dull, decisive thing — they took the census. They walked every ward and wrote down every worker: a name, the household that owned it, the doors its key opened, the task it was hired for, and the date it should be let go. They built a single roll that the whole city could read, and a rule that no new worker could start until it was written into the roll and given an owner. They did not hire fewer workers than the panicking households — in the end they hired far more — but they could always answer the treasurer's question, because they never again let a worker exist that the roll did not know.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Census"
passages.t: The moral is not that the workers were the problem — they did prodigious work, and a city that refused to hire them fell behind. It is that a workforce you have not counted is not an asset; it is an exposure — an unbudgeted cost, an ungoverned key, an unanswerable question when something breaks. The census is not bureaucracy for its own sake. It is the one thing that lets a city keep hiring at scale without losing the ability to govern, pay for, and stand behind the work being done in its name.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Census"
passages.t: The question it forces: We are about to employ a hundred thousand tireless digital workers. So — how many do we run right now? Can we produce, this afternoon, a single roll that names every agent, the human who owns it, the systems its credentials can reach, and the date it should be retired? If we cannot, we are not governing a workforce — we are hoping one governs itself. Are we counting our agents, or only admiring how fast they multiply?

passages.s: 🌐 Cross-sector (any boardroom)
passages.t: - Can we produce an agent census today? Gartner projects 150,000+ agents per Fortune 500 by 2028, yet fewer than half of firms can inventory the agents they run now (SAP LeanIX). If the CEO asked this afternoon "how many agents do we operate, and who owns each," could anyone answer — or would we be a city with no roll? - Is "we're scaling agents fast" an achievement or an exposure? Only ~13% of organizations believe their agent governance is adequate. An uncounted agent is an unbudgeted cost and an ungoverned key — so where is our register, who maintains it, and what stops a new agent from existing before it is written into the roll with an owner? - Who is answerable when an agent we can't name does something we can't explain? The engine is rented; the accountability is not. When an agent alters a record or opens a door, can we trace it to a named agent, a human owner, and an Article-12 log — or does the trail end at "one of our agents, we're not sure which"?

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - Every unregistered agent with a live credential is model risk, access risk and audit risk in one. Do we hold a single register mapping each agent to an owner, a scope of accounts and systems it may touch, and a retirement date — or are there agents holding keys to positions and client data that no inventory knows about? - The regulator will ask "who authorized this and who is accountable." Can we answer at the level of a named agent and a named human — with reconstructable logs (Article 12) — or only at the level of "the platform did it"?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - Agents touching patient records, trial data and care pathways cannot be allowed to accumulate uncounted. Is every clinical or research agent on a governed roll — named, owned, scoped to the minimum data it needs, and retired when its study or workflow ends — or are finished-task agents still holding live access months later? - Accountability for a patient-facing decision must resolve to a person. When an agent acts, can we name the agent, its human owner and its audit trail — or have we deployed a workforce we cannot account for to a regulator or an ethics board?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - Agents on the line, in the supply chain and across OT/IT multiply per site and per team — the definition of sprawl. Do we run one register across plants, or does every site hire its own untracked workers with keys to control systems no central roll can see? - Idle agents are silent cost and silent risk. Do we know which agents finished their task and should be retired — and who is accountable for pruning the roll — or are we paying wages and holding open doors for workers no one remembers hiring?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Agents across storefront, pricing, service and logistics are exactly where sprawl hides behind "it's working." Can we inventory every customer-facing and back-office agent, its owner and its data scope — or is our agent estate growing faster than our ability to see it, one team's quick win at a time? - Token spend and negative-ROI agents drain margin quietly. With ~22% of agent deployments reportedly showing negative ROI at 12 months, do we measure per-agent value and retire the losers — or does the roll only ever grow?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Agents acting on citizen records and statutory process must be countable, owned and auditable by definition. Is there a public-grade register of every agent in service — name, owner, scope, retirement — with Article-12-style reconstructable logs, or are we running ungoverned digital workers over the public's data? - Accountability is not delegable to a vendor. When an agent makes or supports a decision affecting a citizen, can we name the responsible agent and official — or have we lost the roll and, with it, the ability to answer for the state's own actions?

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — Counting the Digital Workforce Before It Counts You
passages.t: Read the stack once more as the parts of an agentic workforce this radar has assembled all week — but now step past building one agent well to the question every enterprise hits the moment it has built more than a handful: do you actually know how many you are running, and can you name each one? The gate admits them; the passport identifies one at the door; the lingua franca lets them speak; the conductor coordinates them; the ear hears their errors; the repertoire is the data they perform. The census is the layer above all of it — the register that turns an uncounted crowd of agents into a governed workforce. The engineering point is blunt: an agent that is not on a register, owned by a human, scoped to least privilege and given a retirement date is not a capability — it is an unmanaged non-human identity with a live credential, and at 150,000 per enterprise that is not an edge case, it is the default.

passages.t: The strategic core: when the agent population is heading to six figures per enterprise and fewer than half of firms can inventory what they already run, "we're scaling agents" describes an exposure, not a moat — the durable capability is the register that lets you scale the workforce while still being able to count, own, scope and retire every member of it. For a week the frame moved from "own the right layer" to "oversee without custody" to "build the gate" to "own the knowledge" to "name the agent" to "speak the open tongue" to "conduct the ensemble" to "keep the ear" to "own the repertoire"; this morning it lands on the discipline that makes all of it governable at scale: count the workforce. "We deploy agents everywhere" is not an answer to "how many do you run and who owns them"; "every agent is on one register — named, owned, scoped to least privilege, logged to the Article-12 standard, and retired when its task ends" is the answer.

Nobody holds the roll (as reported). - The register — the fix everyone is shipping. Count, own, scope, retire (as reported). - The bill — why the board cares. Three-way squeeze (SAP): permissions vs. token spend vs. results; Google Cloud ROI report: 74% claim first-year ROI, ~22% of deployments negative at 12 mo, ~12% of CEOs see both gain and cut. Uncounted agents are uncounted…

passages.s: 7 · So What — Three Moves for the Next 30 Days
passages.t: 1. Take the census — produce one register of every agent you run. You cannot govern what you have not counted. This month, stand up a single source of truth that lists every agent — sanctioned, third-party and shadow — mapped to a human owner, the systems and data its credentials can reach, and the task it was created for. Reconcile it against reality by walking the estate, not by trusting anyone's memory. Report one number to the board: how many agents we actually run today, and how many of them we could name an owner for. If the honest answer is "we don't know," that is the finding. 2. Make registration a gate — no agent runs unless it is on the roll. Sprawl is what happens when creation is easy and counting is optional. Flip it: require that every new agent be registered, owned, and scoped to least privilege before it can touch production — treat an unregistered agent the way you would treat an unbadged employee with a master key. Wire identity and Article-12-style logging into…

passages.t: Tuesday, 1 September 2026 · Cross-sector edition · Audience: C-level + Engineering

passages.s: header
passages.t: Yesterday this radar took the census — the roll that counts every agent you run, names its owner, and scopes what it can touch. This morning the figure the census was always preparing for walks up to the door: the inspector from the capital, asking you to produce the roll and prove it. The EU AI Act's general-purpose-AI obligations became enforceable on 2 August, and within four weeks — on 29 August 2026 — the Commission's AI Office sent its first formal Requests for Information to frontier model providers (reported to include OpenAI, Anthropic and Google), demanding evidence of model security, independent external evaluations, and post-market monitoring (as reported). Compliance stopped being a policy PDF and became a letter with a deadline, backed by fines of up to 3% of global revenue. The board's question this Tuesday: when the inspector asks to see our books — not our intentions, our records — can we produce them this afternoon, agent by agent and log by log, or do we discover…

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: For weeks this radar assembled an agentic workforce and, yesterday, learned to count it. This morning the governing question changes hands: it is no longer do we know how many agents we run? but "can we prove it to someone with the power to fine us?" The answer arrived this week as a hard date. The EU AI Act's GPAI rules became enforceable on 2 August 2026, and on 29 August the Commission's AI Office issued its first formal Requests for Information to frontier providers (reported: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) — the enforcement phase is no longer theoretical (as reported).

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The datable signal — enforcement became real, and it starts at the top of the stack. The first RFIs reportedly cover model security, independent external evaluations, and post-market model monitoring — exactly the evidence an enterprise cannot fabricate after the fact. Fines run to up to 3% of global revenue for GPAI obligations; models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027 to reach full compliance, so the runway is closing, not open (European Commission; law-firm analyses, as reported — several primary pages were unreachable to direct fetch and are relayed via search summaries). The US moved in parallel but opposite in posture: a June 2026 executive order set a voluntary frontier-model framework with an ~1 August deadline and a separate order challenging state AI laws — a lighter federal touch that leaves multinationals managing to the stricter rule, which is Brussels.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The reason it bites now — record spend, flat returns. McKinsey's new State of AI (released ~25 August) became the week's most-cited data point: 40% of $1B+ organizations now say they are scaling AI agents (up from 27% a year earlier), yet only about 6% attribute significant earnings impact to AI and roughly 37% see any EBIT impact — "about the same" share as 2025 (as reported). Spending is at a record — Gartner puts 2026 worldwide AI spend at ~$2.59T (+47%) — while the bottom line barely moves. An avoidable fine lands on a P&L with no cushion, which is exactly why the inspector is a board-level problem and not a legal-department one.

The census (yesterday) is what lets you answer agent-by-agent; the inspection is what tests whether you actually took it.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: Bottom line: the week that built and counted the workforce ends with the authority that will hold you to it. When the inspector asks for your records — not your roadmap, your logs — "we're committed to responsible AI" is not an answer; the register, the reconstructable log, and the named owner per agent are. The firm that took the census can produce the roll in an afternoon and show, agent by agent, who owns it, what it touched and what it did. The firm that only admired the growth discovers, in front of a regulator with a 3%-of-revenue pen, that a workforce it never counted is a workforce it cannot defend. Keep the books before they are asked for — because the inspection is coming whether or not the census was taken, and the exam is graded on the records you have, not the intentions you describe.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Inspector"
passages.t: Topic: This week EU AI Act enforcement stopped being theoretical. General-purpose-AI obligations became enforceable on 2 August 2026, and on 29 August the European Commission's AI Office reportedly sent its first formal Requests for Information to frontier model providers (reported to include OpenAI, Anthropic and Google), covering model security, independent external evaluations and post-market monitoring; fines reach up to 3% of global revenue, and models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027 to reach full compliance. In parallel, a US executive order (June 2026) set a lighter, voluntary frontier-model framework and separately challenged state AI laws, leaving multinationals managing to the stricter EU rule. The pressure that makes it bite is economic: McKinsey's new State of AI (released ~25 August) reports record AI spending with barely-moved earnings — only about 6% of firms attribute significant earnings impact to AI — so an avoidable fine lands…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Inspector"
passages.t: The city had, at last, taken its census. After the autumn it could not count itself, it had walked every ward and built the roll — every worker named, every owner known, every key logged, every finished task retired. The councillors were proud of the register, and rightly; it had been dull, expensive work, and most neighboring cities had never bothered. For a season the roll sat in the treasury, complete and quiet, and the city told itself it was ready.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Inspector"
passages.t: Then, one grey morning, a rider came from the capital. She carried no army and made no threat; she carried a writ. She was the inspector, and her question was not are you a good city or do you mean well. Her question was narrower and far harder to dodge: "Show me your books. For the three workers who touched the granary last month, produce the record — who owned each, what door each key opened, and what each one did. You have until the assizes." She did not want the mayor's speech about responsible governance. She wanted the ledger, opened to the page, on demand.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Inspector"
passages.t: And here the two cities that had looked identical all summer became visible as opposites. The city that had taken the census walked to the treasury, opened the roll to the granary, and laid three names, three owners, three logs on the table before noon. The inspector read them, nodded, and rode on. But the city that had only admired its growth — that had let every household hire through the back door and never kept a roll — stood in the great hall with nothing to hand her. Not because it had done wrong, necessarily, but because it could not show that it hadn't. Its intentions were spotless and entirely unprovable, and an inspector does not grade intentions. She weighed the fine against the city's whole treasury — not the granary, the treasury — and set it at a share of everything the city earned.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Inspector"
passages.t: The cruelty of it was the timing. The city that could not produce its books was the same city whose harvest had come in thin that year: it had spent more than ever on tireless workers and seen its granaries barely fuller than before. It had no slack. A fine it could have avoided entirely — by the dull work of keeping a roll it already knew it should keep — landed on a purse that had nothing spare to pay it. The census would have cost a clerk's wages; the missing census cost a share of the year.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Inspector"
passages.t: The households that had panicked at the first rumor of the inspector did the loud, useless thing: they stopped all the workers, and watched the work stop, and were fined anyway for the records they still could not produce about the months before. The households that kept their footing had done the quiet thing long before the rider was on the road — they had kept the books as they went, so that when the writ finally came, producing the record was not a scramble but a walk to the shelf. They had understood the one thing the panickers never did: you do not pass an inspection you prepare for after the letter arrives. You pass the one you were already keeping books for.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Inspector"
passages.t: The moral is not that the inspector was the enemy — a city with no inspector is a city no one can trust to trade with, and the honest households wanted to be able to prove they were honest. It is that a workforce you cannot document is a workforce you cannot defend, and that the records must exist before they are demanded, because the one thing you can never produce on the day of the assizes is a log you never kept. The census was never bureaucracy for its own sake; it was the city quietly writing the answers to questions it knew would one day be asked by someone with the power to fine.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Inspector"
passages.t: The question it forces: The inspector's letter is already on the road; for the frontier labs it has arrived. So — if a regulator asked us this afternoon to produce, for one agent that touched customer data last month, the reconstructable log of what it did, the human who owns it, and the evidence it was evaluated and monitored, could we lay it on the table before the day is out? Or would we be the city with spotless intentions and no books — fined not for wrongdoing, but for being unable to prove we did none? Are we keeping the records the inspection will ask for, or only hoping we are never asked?

passages.s: 🌐 Cross-sector (any boardroom)
passages.t: - If the inspector's letter arrived tomorrow, could we answer it? The EU AI Office sent its first formal RFIs to frontier labs on 29 August; the enforcement phase is live and fines run to 3% of global revenue. For one agent that touched regulated data last month, can we produce — this afternoon — the reconstructable log, the named human owner, and the evidence it was evaluated and monitored, or do we have spotless intentions and no books? - Are we managing to the stricter rule? The US set a lighter, voluntary frontier framework and is challenging state AI laws, while the EU is now enforcing; a multinational is exposed to Brussels regardless. Have we built to the highest bar our footprint touches (EU AI Act Article 12 logs, Article 50 transparency) — or to the most convenient one, and quietly hoped the inspector rides to someone else's gate first? - Can our P&L absorb an avoidable fine? McKinsey finds record AI spend and barely-moved earnings — only ~6% see significant earnings…

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - The regulator's question is never "did you mean well" — it is "show me the record." When a model or agent makes or supports a decision on credit, positions or client data, can we produce the reconstructable log (Article 12), the named owner, and the evaluation-and-monitoring evidence on demand — or only a policy stating that we care? - External evaluation and post-market monitoring are now enforcement asks, not best practice. Do we hold independent evaluation evidence and live monitoring for every consequential model in production — or would an RFI find a model we cannot currently prove we tested?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - Patient-facing and trial systems draw both a health regulator and, in the EU, the AI Office. Is every clinical or research model logged for reconstructability, disclosed where Article 50 requires, and evidenced with evaluation and monitoring — or would an inspection surface an agent touching patient data whose behavior we cannot reconstruct? - The runway is closing: legacy models have until 2 August 2027. Do we have a dated remediation plan for every pre-2025 model still in service — or are we betting the assizes come after our deadline?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - Agents across OT/IT and the supply chain multiply per site — and each is a record the inspector may ask for. Do we hold one evidence base across plants — logs, owners, evaluations — or does each site keep its own books (or none), so a single RFI becomes a scramble across a dozen jurisdictions? - Documentation is the cheapest insurance in the building. Is compliance evidence generated automatically as agents run — or reconstructed by hand under deadline, which is exactly when it cannot be reconstructed?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Article 50 transparency now bites customer-facing AI: disclosure of AI interaction and labeling of AI-generated content. Are our chat, recommendation and content-generation agents disclosing and labeling as the rule requires — or is a visible, consumer-facing violation the easiest one for a regulator (or a journalist) to find first? - With record spend and thin returns, an avoidable fine is pure margin loss. Do we measure compliance readiness per customer-facing agent the way we measure its ROI — or only discover the gap when someone with authority points at it?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Public bodies are held to the standard they enforce on others. Is there an audit-grade evidence base for every model in citizen-facing service — reconstructable logs, named owners, evaluation and monitoring — that would survive an inspection, not just an internal review? - Accountability is not delegable to a vendor. When a model supports a decision affecting a citizen, can we produce the record and name the responsible official and system — or does the trail end at "the platform did it," which is precisely the answer an inspector will not accept?

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — Keeping the Books Before the Inspector Asks
passages.t: Read the whole stack one more time, but from the outside in — from the seat of the regulator who has just started to knock. The gate admits the agent; the passport names it; the lingua franca lets it speak; the conductor coordinates it; the ear hears its errors; the repertoire is the data it performs; the census counts it. The inspector is the layer above all of it that you do not own and cannot rent: the external authority that arrives and asks you to produce the evidence the other layers were quietly generating. The engineering point is blunt: compliance is not a document you write, it is a byproduct you emit — reconstructable logs, evaluation records, monitoring traces and ownership metadata — generated automatically as every agent runs, because the one artifact you can never manufacture on the day of the audit is a log you never captured.

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — Keeping the Books Before the Inspector Asks
passages.t: - The inspector arrived — enforcement is live. EU AI Act GPAI obligations enforceable since 2 August 2026; the Commission's AI Office reportedly issued its first formal Requests for Information on 29 August to frontier providers (reported: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) on model security, independent external evaluations, and post-market monitoring; fines up to 3% of global revenue; legacy models compliant by 2 August 2027 (as reported; several primary pages unreachable to direct fetch, relayed via search summaries). Read architecturally: the RFI targets the top of the stack first (the model providers), but the obligations flow downstream to every deployer — Article 12 reconstructable logging and Article 50 transparency are enterprise problems, not just lab problems. Build the evidence pipeline now, at the deployer layer, so an upstream RFI does not become a downstream scramble. - The books are an emitted byproduct, not a written document. Article 12 requires automatic event logging…

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — Keeping the Books Before the Inspector Asks
passages.t: The strategic core: when enforcement is live, fines are a share of global revenue, and returns are already thin, "we take responsible AI seriously" is a liability dressed as a virtue — the durable capability is an evidence pipeline that lets you produce, agent by agent, the log, the owner, the evaluation and the monitoring on demand. For weeks the frame moved up the stack — own the layer, oversee without custody, build the gate, own the knowledge, name the agent, speak the open tongue, conduct the ensemble, keep the ear, own the repertoire, take the census; this morning it lands on the one layer that is not yours to design: the authority that grades you. "We are committed to responsible AI" is not an answer to "produce the record for this agent"; "here is the reconstructable log, the named owner, the evaluation evidence and the monitoring trace, generated automatically as it ran" is the answer.

passages.s: Why "the inspector" is the layer that matters now
passages.t: For a year the reflex was to treat compliance as a downstream chore — a policy to publish, a box to check after the capability shipped. This week enforcement reframed it as an evidentiary problem: the question is not whether you are responsible but whether you can prove it, agent by agent, to someone with a 3%-of-revenue pen. What makes a program defensible is not another capability layer but the records the layers below it were already able to emit — the log, the owner, the evaluation, the monitoring. The most valuable move this week is not shipping one more agent; it is being able to answer, on demand and without a scramble, "produce the evidence for this one."

passages.s: How it lands on legacy estates
passages.t: The clean mental model: The model is a rented stove; your proprietary knowledge is the larder; the gateway is the one governed door; the passport names each agent; the lingua franca is the score; the conductor keeps the ensemble in time; the ear hears whether it plays well; the repertoire is the music only your house holds; the census is the roll that counts them. The inspector is the authority above all of it that you cannot rent or design — the one who arrives with a writ and asks you to produce the record, opened to the page. Keep the books before they are asked for.

passages.t: Yesterday the inspector rode in from the capital and asked you to produce the roll — to prove, agent by agent, that every worker was owned, scoped and logged. This morning we learn what the missing roll actually costs, and it is not a fine from a regulator. It is a thief. passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: For a week this radar built an agentic workforce, then learned to count it (the census) and to prove the count to an authority (the inspector). This morning the frame turns from audit to loss: the same ungoverned agent that fails an inspection is the one an attacker walks through — and this week the industry finally attached a number to it. The datable signal is a convergence of enterprise-security data putting a hard, board-legible price on shadow and ungoverned AI: IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach and Kiteworks' 2026 forecast, both re-circulated this week in board-level commentary (Cybersecurity Dive, Alston & Bird, Kiteworks), turned "we should govern our agents" into "here is what not governing them costs (as reported)."

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The number that reframes it — the uncounted agent is not an audit gap, it is a breach vector. IBM's report finds shadow AI implicated in 43% of breaches, up from 20% a year earlier; a shadow-AI breach averaging ~$5.39M and adding as much as ~$670K to the bill; 68% of breached organizations with no AI governance policy; and ~97% lacking proper AI access controls (as reported). The global average breach hit a record ~$4.99M (+12%), and one in four malicious breaches was AI-enabled, each adding roughly $1M. Governance failure — not the technology — is what the data blames.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The reason it is a board problem, not an IT ticket — you cannot stop what you cannot see or reach. Kiteworks' 2026 survey reports 80% of organizations hit by a security or AI incident in the past 12 months, 65% specifically an AI-agent incident, 63% unable to enforce purpose limitations on agents, and 60% unable to terminate a misbehaving one (as reported). Underneath sits the identity math: non-human identities now outnumber humans by roughly 45-to-1 (up to ~144-to-1 in cloud-native estates), while only ~10% of organizations have a mature strategy for them and ~16% do not track AI-identity creation at all (CSA, as reported). The break-in does not force the gate; it walks through the back door the census would have shown and the inspector would have flagged.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: Bottom line: the week that counted the workforce and faced the inspector ends with the cost of skipping both. A workforce you cannot see is a workforce you cannot defend — and this week the industry priced exactly what that costs: a record breach, a shadow-AI premium, and a majority of firms that could not stop an agent gone wrong even if they saw it. The firm that took the census and kept the books does not merely pass an inspection; it closes the door the burglar was counting on. The firm that admired the growth and skipped the roll discovers the missing worker not in an audit room but in an incident report — priced in the treasury, at record rates. Enroll every agent, scope it to least privilege, and hold the kill-switch — because the break-in does not send a letter first, and the door it uses is the one you never wrote down.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Break-In"
passages.t: The city had taken its census, and it had faced the inspector. The councillors thought the hard mornings were behind them — they had counted their tireless workers, named each owner, logged each key, and laid the roll on the table when the writ came. And most of the roll was honest. But a census is only ever as complete as the households that chose to declare, and in the back streets, quietly, some households had gone on hiring the old way: a worker conjured on a whim, given a key to get its errand done, and never entered on any roll. Not out of malice — out of hurry. The work was urgent; the paperwork could wait; and a worker no one wrote down was a worker no one had to explain.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Break-In"
passages.t: Then, one night, there was a break-in at the granary. Not a battering ram at the main gate — the gate was watched, and the watchers were good. The thief did something far simpler: he found the one worker no household had entered on the roll, the one holding a key that opened a door nobody was minding, and he walked in behind it as if he belonged there. By morning the grain was gone. And when the city tried to answer the only questions that mattered — which worker let him in? who owned it? can we take back its key and shut the door before he comes again? — it found it could do none of them. It could not name the worker, because the worker was never on the roll. It could not reach the owner, because none had been assigned. And it could not revoke the key or stop the worker, because you cannot recall a worker you never enrolled and cannot command.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Break-In"
passages.t: And here was the cruelty the census-takers had warned of and the hurried households had waved away: the danger of the unrostered worker was never that it might do wrong on its own. It was that it was a standing, open door — a live key in an unwatched lock — and a door does not have to be malicious to be walked through. The city that had done the dull work could, when the alarm rang, pull the roll, find every worker with a key to the granary, see who owned each, and revoke the keys of any it could not vouch for before the thief returned. The city that had skipped the roll in the back streets stood in the dark counting its losses, unable to say even how many doors it had left open, because it had never written them down. The loss was not theoretical and it was not small: it was weighed, as these things always are, against the treasury — and it came in higher that year than it ever had, because the very households that had hired fastest and counted least were the ones with the most…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Break-In"
passages.t: The households that had panicked at the first alarm did the loud, useless thing: they barred every door at once, and the work stopped, and the thief — who was already inside, wearing a key they still could not find — was untroubled by the barred doors he had never planned to use. The households that kept their footing had done the quiet thing all along: they let no worker exist that the roll did not know, gave each the smallest key that would do its errand, watched every key as closely as they watched the front gate, and kept a hand on a lever that could stop any worker and recall any key in an instant. They understood the one thing the hurried households never did: the front gate you guard is not where the break-in happens. The break-in happens at the door you forgot you had — the one held open by a worker you never wrote down.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Break-In"
passages.t: The moral is not that the workers were treacherous — the overwhelming majority did exactly their errands and nothing more. It is that an unrostered worker is an unlatched door, and a city measured not by its intentions but by its treasury cannot afford to leave doors it cannot see. The census was never bureaucracy; the inspection was never theater; both were the city writing down, in advance, the answers to the questions a break-in asks in the dark — which one, owned by whom, and can you stop it now?

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Break-In"
passages.t: The question it forces: The inspector asks whether we can produce the record; the burglar asks whether we can shut the door. So — if we learned tonight that one agent in our estate was moving data it should not touch, could we, before morning, name it, name its human owner, revoke its credential and stop it — or would we be the city in the dark, counting a record loss against a treasury with no slack, unable even to say how many doors we left open? Do we have a roll, a scope and a kill-switch for every non-human worker with a key — or only a front gate we guard while the back streets hire in the dark?

passages.s: 🌐 Cross-sector (any boardroom)
passages.t: - If an agent went rogue tonight, could we stop it by morning? Kiteworks finds 60% of organizations cannot terminate a misbehaving agent and 63% cannot enforce purpose limits on one. For every agent with a live credential, can we name it, name its human owner, revoke its access and halt it in minutes — or is our kill-switch a hope and a support ticket? - What is our shadow-AI exposure worth? IBM prices a shadow-AI breach at ~$5.39M — roughly $670K above average — with 68% of breached firms carrying no AI governance policy and ~97% lacking AI access controls. Have we quantified our own shadow-AI surface (staff using unapproved AI with sensitive data was found at 65% of firms), or will we first learn its size from an incident report at record breach rates? - Do our non-human identities have owners and expiries? Non-human identities outnumber humans ~45:1 (to ~144:1 in cloud), yet ~10% of firms are mature on them and ~16% do not even track AI-identity creation. Is every agent…

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - A single ungoverned agent with market or client-data access is a standing open door. Can we produce, for every agent touching money or PII, its owner, its scoped permission and a working revocation path — or would a break-in find an agent we cannot name, own or stop? - Materiality and disclosure now attach to AI incidents. If an agent incident crossed the materiality threshold tomorrow, could we reconstruct what it did and contain it before it became an 8-K event — or only after?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - Patient data and clinical systems are exactly the intellectual-property and PII shadow-AI breaches expose most. Is every clinical or research agent enrolled, scoped to least privilege and monitored — or would an unrostered agent be the quiet door into the most sensitive records we hold? - The reflex to "add more agents faster" outruns the ability to govern them. Do we gate deployment on enrollment and a kill-switch, or do we ship first and discover the ungoverned agent when it leaks?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - Agents across OT/IT and the supply chain multiply per site, and each is a credential in a lock. Do we hold one enrolled, owned, revocable inventory of agent identities across plants — or does each site hire in the back streets, so we cannot say how many open doors we have? - A stopped line and a stolen design cost the same treasury. Can we revoke a compromised agent's access across every site at once, or only plant by plant while the thief is already inside?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Customer-facing chat, recommendation and content agents are the most exposed and the easiest to spin up in the shadows. Are all of them enrolled, scoped and monitored — or is a consumer-facing agent leaking PII the break-in a journalist finds before we do? - Shadow AI is now the top driver of negligent-insider incidents. Do we measure staff use of unapproved AI on customer data the way we measure conversion — or only after the breach is priced?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Public bodies hold citizen data and are held to the standard they set. Is there an enrolled, owned, revocable register of every agent in citizen-facing service, with a working kill-switch — or would a break-in expose an agent we cannot name or stop? - Accountability is not delegable to a vendor or an agent. When an agent acts, can we name the responsible official and revoke the agent's key — or does the trail end at "the system did it," which is the door a thief relies on?

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — Shutting the Door Before the Break-In
passages.t: Read the whole stack one more time, but from the seat of the attacker instead of the regulator. The gate admits the agent; the passport names it; the lingua franca lets it speak; the conductor coordinates it; the ear hears its errors; the repertoire is the data it performs; the census counts it; the inspector asks you to produce the count. The break-in is what the missing entries actually cost: every agent you did not enroll is a live, non-human credential in a lock nobody is minding — and this week the industry finally priced it. The engineering point is blunt: the front gate is not where you get breached; you get breached at the door held open by an agent that was never enrolled, never scoped, and cannot be stopped — so the durable control is not a bigger wall but a smaller key, a watched lock, and a lever that recalls it.

Read architecturally: the cost is not attributed to the model's behavior but to the absence of enrollment, scope and control around it. passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — Shutting the Door Before the Break-In
passages.t: The strategic core: when the ungoverned agent is priced at record breach rates and a majority of firms cannot even stop one, "we'll add security later" is a debt that compounds into the incident report — the durable capability is an enrolled, least-privileged, revocable identity for every non-human worker, watched as closely as the front gate. For weeks the frame climbed the stack — own the layer, build the gate, own the knowledge, name the agent, speak the open tongue, conduct the ensemble, keep the ear, own the repertoire, take the census, face the inspector; this morning it turns to the adversary who benefits from every gap the others leave. "We have a firewall" is not an answer to "which agent let him in, who owns it, and can you stop it"; "here is the agent, its owner, its scope, and the lever that just revoked its key" is the answer.

passages.s: Why "the break-in" is the layer that matters now
passages.t: For a year the reflex was to treat agent security as perimeter security — a bigger wall, a stricter firewall, a policy PDF. This week the data reframed it as an identity and control problem: the breach does not come over the wall; it comes through a non-human credential you never enrolled and cannot revoke. What contains a break-in is not another perimeter layer but the records and controls the layers below could already emit — the enrolled identity, the named owner, the least-privilege scope, the working kill-switch. The most valuable move this week is not adding one more agent; it is being able to answer, in the dark and in minutes, "which agent, owned by whom, and can you stop it now?"

passages.s: How it lands on legacy estates
passages.t: The clean mental model: The model is a rented stove; your proprietary knowledge is the larder; the gateway is the one governed door; the passport names each agent; the lingua franca is the score; the conductor keeps the ensemble in time; the ear hears whether it plays well; the repertoire is the music only your house holds; the census is the roll that counts them; the inspector is who asks you to produce the roll. The break-in is what the missing entries cost — a thief through the door held open by a worker you never enrolled and cannot stop. Enroll every agent, give it the smallest key, watch every lock, and keep a hand on the lever.

This morning the frame turns from risk to return: now that everyone can deploy agents, who is actually making money from them — and why is almost no one? The datable signal is a convergence around a single figure: McKinsey's State of AI 2026, re-circulated this week (2 Sep, AIwire / BigDATAwire) under the frame "enterprise AI is becoming a two-speed race," reporting record agent adoption against flat earnings impact — the classic mark of motion without milling (as reported).

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Mills"
passages.t: There were two mills on the same river, drawing from the same current, grinding the same grain. In a year when everyone suddenly wanted flour, both millers did the obvious thing: they built. They fixed more paddles to their wheels, they hired more hands, they set the water rushing harder than it ever had, and from the road both mills looked magnificent — wheels roaring, spray flying, a great noise of industry that made the whole valley feel prosperous. The first miller, watching his wheel turn faster than his father's ever had, was certain the flour would follow the motion. It had to. Look how it turned.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Mills"
passages.t: But at harvest, when the sacks were counted, the two mills told very different stories. The first miller's sacks were nearly as empty as the year before — a little more, perhaps, but nothing like the roar of the wheel had promised. The second miller's storehouse was full. And the strange thing, the thing that kept the first miller up at night, was that they had the same river, the same grain, and if anything his wheel turned faster. So he walked downstream to see what his neighbor had done differently, expecting to find a bigger wheel, a stronger current, some secret paddle. He found none of it. The second miller's wheel was ordinary. What was different was everything between the wheel and the stone.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Mills"
passages.t: For the second miller had understood the one thing the first never did: a mill does not grind flour by turning. It grinds flour when the turning of the wheel is carried, through gearing built for the purpose, into a millstone dressed to bite the grain. The first miller had spent all his money on the wheel and none on the works. His river's power spun the axle magnificently and then dissipated into noise, because the gearing was the same gearing his grandfather had cut for a slower wheel, and the millstone was smooth from a decade of use and bit nothing. He had more motion than any mill on the river and less milling, because motion that never reaches the stone is just expensive spray. The second miller had done the unglamorous, invisible thing: he had torn out the old gearing and rebuilt the entire works around the new wheel — re-cut the cogs so the power actually transferred, re-dressed the stone so it bit, changed where the grain entered and where the flour came out — so that…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Mills"
passages.t: The millers who panicked at the empty sacks did the loud, useless thing: they built bigger wheels. If motion had not produced flour, surely more motion would — so they doubled the paddles, dammed the river higher, and roared louder than ever into the same unchanged works, and the sacks stayed empty, and the money ran out, and one by one the great noisy wheels were left to rot because a wheel that grinds nothing is only a cost. The millers who prospered had learned the quiet truth their neighbors would not hear: you do not get more flour by spinning the wheel faster over the old works. You get it by rebuilding the works so the wheel you already have actually reaches the stone. The river was the same for everyone. What separated a full storehouse from an empty one was never the size of the wheel — it was whether anyone had done the dull, expensive labor of re-cutting the gearing and dressing the stone.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Mills"
passages.t: The moral is not that the wheel does not matter — you cannot grind without one. It is that the wheel is the cheap part and the loud part, and the works are the hard part and the quiet part, and only the works turn motion into flour. Everyone bought the wheel; almost no one rebuilt the works; and at harvest the valley divided cleanly into the few storehouses that were full and the many that were merely loud.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Mills"
passages.t: The question it forces: Our wheel is turning faster than it ever has — more agents deployed, more pilots running, more spend than last year. So the only question that matters at harvest: how much more flour do we actually have? Can we name one process we redesigned end to end around agents — fewer steps, different handoffs, humans on the exceptions — and point to the EBIT line it moved? Or have we, like most of the valley, spent all our money on a magnificent wheel bolted to the same old works, mistaking the roar for the flour? Are we in the 6% that rebuilt the works, or the 94% still waiting for motion to become milling?

passages.s: 🌐 Cross-sector (any boardroom)
passages.t: - Where is our flour? McKinsey finds ~6% of firms are AI high performers and only ~37% see any EBIT impact, "about the same" as last year — while 40% of large firms are scaling agents. Can we point to a single EBIT line that AI moved this year, or are we running a faster wheel over the same works and calling the noise progress? - Did we rebuild the works, or just add paddles? High performers are ~3× more likely to fundamentally redesign workflows end to end. For our biggest AI bet, did we redesign the process — fewer steps, different handoffs, humans on the exceptions — or did we lay an agent over a workflow built for people and hope? - Which pilots are cost lines waiting to be cut? Gartner expects 40% of agentic projects canceled by end 2027 on unclear value. Have we tied every agent in production to a measurable business result with an owner — or are some of ours "agent washing" we will quietly shut down next year?

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - Automation ROI here is real but concentrated in redesigned processes (underwriting, reconciliation, servicing). Have we re-cut the gearing — rebuilt the workflow around the agent — for one high-volume process, or bolted a copilot onto a process still shaped for human handoffs? - Cost discipline is a board reflex. Can we show, per agent program, the flour — cycle-time cut, loss avoided, revenue added — against the spend, or only the number of pilots underway?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - Clinical and research workflows are dense with handoffs — exactly where rewiring, not overlay, produces value. Have we redesigned one clinical or R&D process end to end around agents, or are we measuring "AI adoption" by seats and pilots rather than by outcomes and throughput? - The safety bar makes half-built projects expensive. Do we kill an agent pilot that cannot show a validated result, or let it run because it looks modern while grinding no flour?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - The mill metaphor is literal here: motion at the wheel is not output at the stone. Do we measure agent programs by throughput and yield at the process, or by activity — tokens, tasks, pilots — that never reaches the P&L? - Standardization across sites is where redesign compounds. Have we rebuilt one workflow around agents and rolled the redesigned process (not just the tool) across plants, or does each site bolt agents onto its own old works?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Customer-facing agents multiply fastest and show ROI last without redesign. Have we rebuilt the service or merchandising process around the agent — or added a chatbot to a journey still designed for a call center? - Build-vs-buy is now live: 32% of firms skip software to build with agentic coding tools. Where we build, are we redesigning the workflow it serves — or just re-creating the old tool with a faster wheel?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Value must be demonstrable and auditable, not asserted. For each citizen-facing agent, can we show the redesigned process and the outcome it improved — or only that we "deployed AI"? - Cancelled projects are public failures. Do we gate agent programs on a redesigned process and a measurable result before scaling — or discover at audit that the wheel turned and the flour never came?

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — Rebuilding the Works, Not the Wheel
passages.t: Read the whole stack one more time, but from the seat of the treasurer counting sacks at harvest. The gate admits the agent; the passport names it; the lingua franca lets it speak; the conductor coordinates it; the ear hears its errors; the repertoire is the data it performs; the census counts it; the inspector asks you to produce the count; the break-in is what the missing entries cost. The two mills are what all of it is for: turning the motion of a deployed agent into flour on the P&L — and this week the data showed that for all but ~6% of firms, the motion is not yet reaching the stone. The engineering point is blunt: an agent laid over a process designed for humans produces expensive motion, not milling; the value comes from re-cutting the gearing — redesigning the workflow end to end so the agent's output actually lands as a business result — which is the hard, quiet, un-demoable part almost everyone skips.

This morning the model layer itself moved, loudly: capability is commoditizing in real time, and the cheapest capability is now sold for data instead of dollars. passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The number that frames it — the wheel is nearly free now. On 2–3 September the trade press reported AI token prices collapsing ~60% in a single window (Tech Startups, 3 Sep), extending a multi-year slide that has taken GPT-4-class quality from ~$30 to under $0.50 per million tokens and Google's Flash line down ~99.7% in three years (as reported). Three frontier-class releases landed almost on top of each other — Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 (26 Aug; Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 66, the current top), Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash (1 Sep; $0.75 / $3.75 per million), and Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 (2 Sep; Index 62 for the preview "max," 61 for the shipping "xhigh," behind only Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5) (as reported). The rented stove is now a near-commodity. Renting it is no longer where the money — or the risk — lives.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)

Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 lists a Standard tier at $1.25 / $4.25 per million tokens (no training on your data) and a Contributor tier at $0.10 / $0.20 — up to ~21× cheaper — whose discount is granted in exchange for permission to train on your prompts and completions (as reported). Meta's own terms tell users not to submit sensitive, confidential or personal information to the discounted tier. passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: Bottom line: the week that built, counted, inspected, secured and finally questioned the value of the agentic workforce ends where the whole stack begins — the model — and finds it collapsing toward free. But "free" is a pricing tier, not a fact: the cheapest tokens in the market are now sold for training rights on your own prompts, and the switch that buys them is a config string, not a contract. The mill in the old country never charged coin; it took the multure — a fixed handful of every sack it ground — and the miller who ground cheapest kept the biggest toll, learned every household's recipe from the grain that passed through, and in time sold their own bread back to them. Price your model tiers in data as well as dollars, make the training-tier model id a governed procurement decision rather than a config default, and keep your proprietary grain out of the cheap mill — because the wheel is finally almost free, and that is exactly when you pay with something dearer than money.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Miller's Toll"
passages.t: In the old country a miller did not ask for coin. He asked for the multure — the toll — a fixed portion scooped from every sack of grain that passed under his stone, and out of those scoops he made his living. So when a household carried its wheat to be ground, it paid not in money but in flour: a handful here, a measure there, taken from the very grain it brought. For most of a lifetime this seemed a fair and settled thing, because the toll was small and the grinding was necessary, and no one thought very hard about the slow river of everyone's grain running quietly into one man's storehouse.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Miller's Toll"
passages.t: Then a season came when new mills sprang up all along the river, one after another in the space of a few days, each grinding faster and finer than the last, until the grinding that had once been dear was suddenly almost free. And into that crowd stepped a miller who made an offer no one had heard before. Bring your grain to me, he said, and I will grind it for almost nothing — a tenth of what the others charge, less than the cost of the water. The households could not believe their luck, and the queues at his gate ran long. Only the careful few asked the question that mattered: if he charges almost no coin, what is he living on? And the answer was the oldest answer in milling. He was living on the toll. He had simply moved it out of sight. The cheap miller took barely a coin — but from every sack he kept a generous handful, and he did something with those handfuls that the old millers never had: he studied them. He learned which household grew which wheat, whose grain made the…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Miller's Toll"
passages.t: The dear miller up the road, the one who still charged honest coin and kept not a single grain that was not his, watched the queues pass him by and said nothing, because he understood what his neighbors did not: the cheapest mill was not cheap. It had only changed what it charged. It took its price in grain instead of coin, and grain — your grain, your seed, your recipe — is dearer than coin, because coin buys one loaf and grain buys every loaf you will ever bake. The households that flocked to the cheap gate thought they were saving money. They were paying the most expensive toll in the valley, and they were paying it in the one thing they could never buy back.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Miller's Toll"
passages.t: And here was the cruelest part, the part that undid even careful households: the toll was invisible. There was no contract to sign at the cheap mill, no ledger, no moment where a steward looked up and said this sack will be tolled in grain. There was only which gate your cart happened to roll through — and the gates stood side by side, unmarked, so that a single hired hand, sent down with the morning's grain and told merely to use the cheap mill, it's faster, could route a season's harvest into the tolling gate without anyone in the household ever deciding to. By the time the master noticed, the grain was already ground, the handfuls already scooped, the recipe already learned. You cannot refuse a toll you never saw yourself agree to.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Miller's Toll"
passages.t: The households that kept their footing did the unglamorous thing. They did not swear off the cheap mill entirely — the grinding was genuinely good, and coin saved is coin saved. But they wrote down, plainly, which grain could go to the tolling gate and which could not. The common wheat, the grain whose recipe was no secret, the flour anyone in the valley could already make — that they sent to the cheap mill gladly and pocketed the savings. But the seed stock, the heirloom strain, the recipe that was the whole reason anyone bought their bread — that grain went only to the dear mill that took coin and kept nothing, and it went there by rule, not by the whim of whoever happened to be driving the cart. They priced their grain in two currencies at once — coin and toll — and they decided, deliberately and in advance, which sacks they were willing to pay for in each.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Miller's Toll"
passages.t: The question it forces: The model just got cheaper than it has ever been — three frontier labs shipped in a week and token prices fell by more than half. So the question is not "are we getting a good price," it is "what are we paying with?" Do we know which of our AI workloads run on a data-tolling tier — a Contributor model id, a default-on training setting, a free plan that trains on our content? Can any engineer flip a production workload onto the cheap mill with one config string, or is the tolling model id a governed procurement decision with a named owner? And have we actually written down which of our data is common wheat we will happily trade for cheap tokens, and which is the seed stock that must never pass through a mill that keeps a handful — or are we, like most of the valley, carting our whole harvest to the cheapest gate because the coin price looked too good to ask what the real toll was?

passages.s: 🌐 Cross-sector (any boardroom)

Token prices fell ~60% in a single window this week, and the cheapest tier on the market (Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor, $0.10/$0.20) is discounted up to ~21× in exchange for training on your prompts and completions. Do we know which of our AI workloads run on a data-tolling tier — and did anyone decide that on purpose, or did it arrive as a config default? - Can one config string move us onto the cheap mill? The tolling tier is a different model id, not a contract or an account setting — no procurement step, no audit trail until someone greps the config. Is our training-tier model id a governed procurement decision with a named owner, or can any engineer flip a production workload onto it unnoticed? - Which of our data is common wheat, and which is seed stock? Free and discounted tiers now train on your content by default across the stack (Atlassian Rovo defaulted ~300k orgs on 17 Aug). Have we written down, in advance, which data may pass through…

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - Customer records, transaction data and proprietary models are regulated seed stock, not common wheat. Do we have a hard control that blocks data-tolling model ids (Contributor tiers, train-by-default free plans) from touching regulated data — enforced at the gateway, not asked of the developer? - The cheap-token temptation lands hardest on high-volume, low-margin automation. Where we chase the ~21× discount, can we prove the workload carries only non-sensitive grain — or are we tolling customer data to shave inference cost?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - PHI and proprietary research are the definition of grain you can never buy back. Does any pathway exist by which a clinician's or researcher's prompt could reach a train-on-your-data tier — and can we prove it is closed, given the switch is a model id an engineer controls? - The savings are real and the pressure to capture them is real. Have we designated which non-clinical, non-identifiable workflows may use the cheap mill, so the discount is captured deliberately rather than the sensitive data leaking into it by accident?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - Process data, yields and designs are the recipe competitors would pay for. Do our engineering and design tools default to a Standard (no-training) model id, or could a Contributor-tier config string route proprietary process data into a vendor's training set? - Commoditizing model prices are a genuine cost win at industrial token volumes. Have we split our workloads — common wheat to the cheap mill, seed stock to the dear one — so we bank the savings without tolling the designs?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Customer behavior, pricing and assortment logic are exactly the "recipe" the cheap miller learns and resells. Are our customer-facing and merchandising agents pinned to no-training model ids, or are we trading tomorrow's competitive edge for today's cheaper tokens? - Consumer free tiers train by default too. Do we know which shadow, employee-adopted AI tools are grinding company data at a tolling gate for free — and can we even see them?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Citizen data tolled into a vendor's training set is a headline, not a saving. Can we demonstrate, to an auditor, that no public-service workload runs on a train-on-your-data tier — by policy and by enforced control, not by developer good intent? - Procurement is the natural gate. Have we made the tolling model id a procurement-and-approval decision, so the cheapest tier cannot enter production as a quiet config change?

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — Pricing the Model in Two Currencies
passages.t: Read the whole stack one more time, but from the seat of the person signing the model bill — and paying a second, invisible bill they never see. The gate admits the agent; the passport names it; the lingua franca lets it speak; the conductor coordinates it; the ear hears its errors; the repertoire is the data it performs; the census counts it; the inspector asks for the count; the break-in is what the missing entries cost; the two mills are whether the motion grinds flour. The miller's toll is what the model layer underneath all of it now charges — because this week the model rented for almost nothing, and the cheapest rent is paid not in dollars but in the right to train on your data. The engineering point is blunt: a model tier is now two prices at once — a dollar price per token and a data price in training rights — and the second price is set by a model id, invisible to every dashboard that only tracks the first.

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — Pricing the Model in Two Currencies
passages.t: The strategic core: when the model commoditizes toward free, value and risk both migrate to your data — and the cheapest model tier is the market's most efficient mechanism for acquiring it. For weeks the frame climbed the stack — own the layer, build the gate, own the knowledge, name the agent, speak the open tongue, conduct the ensemble, keep the ear, own the repertoire, take the census, face the inspector, shut the break-in, rebuild the mill's works. This morning it returns to the foundation and finds the ground shifting: the model is nearly free, and "nearly free" is a tier with a toll. "We got a great price on tokens" is not the whole sentence; the whole sentence is "we got a great price on tokens, and here is the data we agreed to pay with, and here is the control that keeps our seed stock out of the cheap mill."

passages.s: Why "the miller's toll" is the layer that matters now
passages.t: For two years the reflex was to treat the model as the expensive, differentiating part of the stack — pick the best one, pay the premium, guard the API key. This week broke that frame in public: capability is commoditizing toward free, and once the dollar price of a token approaches zero, the only price left to charge is your data. The cheapest tier on the market is now, explicitly, a data-acquisition instrument dressed as a discount. What separates a firm that banks the commoditization win from one that quietly hands over its moat is not a better model or a bigger budget — it is the discipline to price every model tier in two currencies, to classify data as common wheat or seed stock, and to enforce the split at the gateway rather than trust it to whoever writes the config.

passages.s: header
passages.t: Yesterday the model layer commoditized in public and we learned the cheapest tier is paid for in your data. This morning the story moves one turn deeper: the tools have started improving the tools. In a paper re-circulated this week, Anthropic reported that nine Claude Opus 4.6 agents, running in parallel for five days, recovered ~97% of the performance gap on a real alignment problem — where two of its own senior researchers, given seven days, recovered ~23% — at a total cost of about $18,000, or ~$22 per agent-hour (as reported). In the same window OpenAI unveiled Jalapeño, its first custom inference chip, co-developed with Broadcom from design to tape-out in ~nine months — believed the fastest high-performance ASIC cycle ever — with OpenAI's own models used to accelerate the design (as reported), and Google says long-running agentic loops now help evaluate and refine its models. AI is now doing AI's research and designing AI's silicon. But the same week's sober counter-signal…

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: For two weeks this radar climbed the stack — built the agentic workforce, named it, counted it, faced the inspector, priced the break-in, asked whether the motion grinds flour, and watched the model commoditize toward free. This morning the frame turns a corner: the newest capability is not a better worker but a worker that improves the workshop. AI is now doing meaningful parts of AI research and hardware design — and that compounds capability, but it also compounds whatever error, bias or drift rides along in the loop, while quietly lifting the human who could vouch for the standard out of it.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The number that frames it — the apprentice out-worked the masters. In a result re-circulated this week, Anthropic's "automated researchers" — nine Claude Opus 4.6 agents in parallel sandboxes, sharing findings, running five days — recovered ~97% of the maximum performance gap on an open alignment problem, versus ~23% for two of Anthropic's own senior researchers given seven days, at ~$18,000 total (~$22 per agent-hour) (as reported). Alongside it, OpenAI's Jalapeño inference chip (with Broadcom) went from design to tape-out in ~nine months, its development sped up by OpenAI's own models (as reported), and Google reports agentic loops helping refine its models. The tools are improving the tools.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The catch that makes it a board issue — the standard is now passed apprentice-to-apprentice. The same coverage carries the caveat that keeps this honest: the automated researchers' best discovered method did not transfer as a statistically significant improvement to a different model (Claude Sonnet 4), and the task was picked for unusually clean scoring (as reported) — i.e., the clever trick from the fastest apprentice did not hold up on the next bench. This is not yet autonomous recursive self-improvement (MIT Technology Review, 18 Aug: humans remain deeply involved; many figures are company-reported). The enterprise risk is not runaway superintelligence; it is provenance and vouching — as AI-built AI enters your stack, can you still say who taught what to whom, and stand behind the mark on the newest work? The regulator is about to ask literally that: GPAI systemic-risk evaluations are due to the EU AI Office on 15 September (as reported).

On 15 September, GPAI providers above 10²⁵ FLOPs must file their first formal systemic-risk evaluations with the EU AI Office — red-teaming methods, energy disclosures, copyright-training summaries — under an Act live since 2 August, fines to €35M or 7% of global turnover (as reported).
