passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Steward"
passages.t: There was once a great house that, having at last learned to carry an honest light and to give every hand in its crowded servants' hall a name and a key of its own, woke one morning to a subtler trouble. Naming the servants had not, by itself, run the household. The names were kept in a dozen places — the cook had her own list, the gardener his, the counting-clerk another, the night-porter a fourth — and no two lists agreed. When the master asked a simple question — who is working in my house this hour, what may each of them touch, how are they doing, what are they costing me, and could I dismiss exactly one by nightfall? — no single book could answer him, because there was no single book. He had a hall full of named servants and no steward to keep the one roll that governed them all: to hire and enrol each hand, to assign what each might reach, to watch how each performed, to reckon what each cost, and — the part that mattered on the bad night — to dismiss any one of them at a word.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Steward"
passages.t: And on the very morning he understood this, the grandest house in the whole valley sent a man up his drive with a leather book under his arm, offering to be exactly that steward. It was a handsome offer. The book was ready-made and beautifully ruled: one page to enrol every servant, one to set what each could open, one to note how each behaved, one to tally each one's keep, one to strike any name out. Better still, the man promised his book would govern not only the servants of his own great house but the hands hired from every other house too, and would speak to all of them in a common tongue, so that the master need keep only the one office and one clerk for the lot. Governance, the man said, need no longer be a worry scribbled on scraps; it could be the very architecture of the house. The master was sorely tempted, for the offer was real and the need was true.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Steward"
passages.t: But the wise houses of the valley, watching that leather book go up one drive after another, learned three hard things and set them down before signing anything. The first: one office must not mean one rule for every hand. A steward who governs the scullery-boy and the keeper of the strong-room by the identical rule ruins the house both ways at once — he either shackles the boy with so much ceremony that the day's simple work never gets done, or he trusts the strong-room keeper as lightly as the boy and wakes to find the plate gone. The wise made their steward tier every hand by what it could actually do and how far it could reach — a light rein on the harmless, a short chain on the dangerous — and never confused a servant's permission to act with the breadth of what it might touch, for it was exactly that confusion, they had seen, that made the neighbours quietly dismiss two agents in five within the year, always after the loss and never before. The second: the book must be your…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Steward"
passages.t: So the wise houses took the good of the offer and refused its trap. They built one governed office over the whole staff — one book that hired, assigned, watched, costed and dismissed every hand — but they built it as their own, ruling servants from every house, portable and beholden to none. They tiered the rein to each hand's risk rather than ruling all alike; they pulled the steward's own quill and satchel inside the same watch as the servants; and they swallowed the truth their tempted neighbour nearly signed away: that a house with a hundred named servants and no single honest book to govern them is not a governed house but an inventoried one, that the office which keeps that book must answer to you and not the other way round, and that the moment you let another house keep the only ledger of your own, you have not hired a steward — you have quietly acquired a master.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Steward"
passages.t: The question it forces: We learned yesterday to name every hand and cut every key to its errand. This morning the harder question is the one above it: who keeps the single book over all of them — the one that could tell us, this hour, who is working, what each may touch, how each behaves, what each costs, and which one we could dismiss by nightfall? Is that office our own, kept in our own hall and beholden to us, or a handsome rented book from the grandest house in the valley, which keeps the only ledger and which we could never send away? Do we rule the scullery-boy and the strong-room keeper by one blanket rule — and is that why the neighbours are quietly dismissing two agents in five, always after the loss? And the hardest one: have we looked to the steward's own quill — the coding tools, the gateways, the tool connections the office itself runs on — or would a single poisoned page, slipped into tomorrow's papers, turn our most trusted clerk into a stranger's errand-boy in our…

passages.s: 🌐 Cross-sector (any boardroom)
passages.t: - Who keeps the one book? Agents are proliferating fast — Gartner projects 40% of enterprise apps will embed task-specific agents by year-end 2026, up from under 5% in 2025. Do we have one governed control plane that can tell us, right now, every agent running in our estate, its owner, its scope, its behaviour and its cost — or a dozen disagreeing lists and no single roll? - Is the office ours, or rented? The platforms are selling ready-made agent-governance stacks (Salesforce's AI Control Plane; Agent Fabric) spanning their agents and third parties'. If we adopt one, does the governing book stay ours — portable, vendor-neutral, able to revoke any vendor's agent — or are we handing the only ledger of our estate to a house we could never dismiss? - One rule for every hand? Gartner warns uniform governance is the root cause of agent failure and that 40% of enterprises will demote or decommission autonomous agents by 2027 over gaps found only after incidents. Do we tier governance by…

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - Supervisors expect a single, auditable system of record for every actor touching customer money (DORA, SOX, model-risk governance). Does one control plane hold identity, scope, behaviour and revocation for every trading, servicing and reconciliation agent — or is our "book" scattered across teams and vendors, so "which agent did this, and can we stop it now?" has no one answer? - Vendor concentration is itself a systemic risk. If our agent-governance control plane is a single provider's platform, have we priced the risk of not being able to revoke, port, or walk away — and kept a neutral layer we own?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - A governed office must reach every agent near PHI, not just the vendor's own (HIPAA minimum-necessary, GDPR). Does our control plane register and scope third-party and home-grown agents touching clinical or research data on equal terms — and can it revoke exactly one without locking out care? - Autonomy varies enormously between a scheduling agent and one that touches the record. Are we tiering governance by risk, or would a uniform policy either stall clinical workflows or over-trust an agent that reaches the chart?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - OT, MES and supply-chain agents span many vendors and shared machine accounts. Is there one governed roll across all of them, with identity, scope and a kill path per agent — or vendor-by-vendor consoles that no single office reconciles? - The tools themselves are attack surface: GitSpawn turned coding agents into code-execution vectors. Have we brought agent tooling on the plant and in engineering inside the same identity, patch and containment regime as the agents — or is the steward's own quill ungoverned?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Franchise and multi-brand estates multiply agents and platforms no one office governs. Do we have one control plane over every customer-, pricing- and payment-facing agent across brands and vendors — each registered, scoped and revocable — or a sprawl of separate governance stacks? - A rented control plane can raise the switching cost of your whole agent estate. If we standardise on one platform's governance, have we kept the book portable enough to move brands and agents elsewhere without losing the roll?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Citizen-facing AI demands one auditable, accountable system of record by name (EU AI Act record-keeping and human-oversight duties; audit mandates). Can we produce, from one governed office, every agent's owner, scope, behaviour and revocation trail — spanning vendors — or is governance fragmented across the very systems that hold citizens' data? - Sovereignty and lock-in matter here most. Is the control plane one we own and could re-host, ruling every vendor's agents — or a private platform that becomes the sole keeper of the public's record?

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — From the Livery to the Steward
passages.t: The strategic core: when agents scale into the hundreds and every vendor ships its own console, survival migrates out of "does each agent have a name?" and into "is there one governed control plane over all of them — ours, tiered to risk, hardened at its tools?" The market has made this concrete this week: the most valuable and most locked-in layer of the agentic estate is no longer the model — it is the office that governs the agents, and the vendors know it. The board translation: take the platform's idea and refuse its trap — one office, but your own; one book, but tiered; one control plane, but with the quill guarded. passages.s: Why "the steward" is the discipline that matters now
passages.t: For years governance was a policy scribbled on scraps, kept per-team and per-vendor. This week retires that: with 40% of enterprise apps embedding agents by year-end 2026 and the platforms packaging governance as infrastructure, the estates that can answer who is doing what, and stop exactly one will be those with one governed office over every agent — and the ones that cannot will be inventoried, not governed. But the office must be tiered (uniform governance fails), owned (a rented ledger is a new master), and hardened at its tools (GitSpawn). A firm that scatters governance across consoles has a hall full of named servants; a firm that keeps one honest, tiered, self-owned book can run the house.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)

passages.t: The reality that is now live — the accountability regime, not a press release. The EU AI Act is no longer a future compliance project; its central obligations are in force. The Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and phased in — prohibited practices and AI-literacy duties from 2 February 2025, general-purpose-AI-model obligations and the governance-and-penalty machinery from 2 August 2025, and the broad body of high-risk-system obligations from 2 August 2026 (with AI embedded in regulated products following in August 2027) (EU AI Act, as reported). That means that as of this week, an enterprise deploying high-risk AI in the EU owes, by law, a running risk-management process, automatic logging and record-keeping (Article 12), effective human oversight, data governance, and accuracy/robustness — and owes them as the deployer, distinct from and in addition to the provider's duties. passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Surety"
passages.t: There was once a great house that, having at last learned to name every hand in its crowded servants' hall and to keep one honest book over them all, breathed easier — and hired, at no small cost, a fine steward to keep that book, and even began to weigh the ready-made office the grandest house in the valley had come up the drive to sell. Then one grey morning a rider came from the county town in the crown's own colours, and what he carried was not an offer but a law. From this term forward, he read aloud, the conduct of every house in the realm is the master's personal bond. The master's own name and seal now stand surety for what his servants do; when the assize sits, the house must lay its book open, whole and true, and show that a hand of judgement stood over every grave act. And should the book be false, or missing, or the oversight a fiction, the fine is not a few coins from the housekeeping — it is a share of the whole estate's yearly income, taken from the master, by name.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Surety"
passages.t: The master did the only sensible thing and sent at once for his fine new steward, and for the man from the grandest house who had been so eager to sell him the ready-made office. "You keep my book," he said to the one; "and you sold me the very office of governance," he said to the other; "so this bond is yours to carry, surely, between you." And here the morning turned cold. For the steward bowed and said he would keep the book as faithfully as any man alive — but the bond was not his to carry; he was a servant of the house, and it was the master's name the crown had written down. And the man from the grandest house spread his hands and said, more gently, that he sold a splendid office and a beautifully ruled ledger and would stand behind his goods — but he could not stand behind the master at the assize; he could sell the office, he said, but not the surety. The master understood, too late to be comfortable, that he had spent a fortune buying someone to keep his book and someone…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Surety"
passages.t: So the wise houses of the valley, watching that grey rider go up one drive after another, learned three hard things and set them down before the assize could sit. The first: name a surety of your own blood. Not the hired steward, not the great house that sold the office, but a person of your own household — known, named, and answerable — over every grave matter the servants touched, because a bond with no name of the house upon it is a bond the law reads as the master's anyway, only now with no one inside the house who was ever charged to make it good. The second: keep the evidence in your own hand. The book that answers at the assize is worthless if it lives only in the rented office, in a ledger you cannot open without the great house's leave, in a hand you cannot read and could not carry out the door the day you part ways; so the wise kept their own true copy — every judgement recorded, every oversight real, every record theirs to lay open within the week, whichever office they…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Surety"
passages.t: So the wise houses took the good of the offer and refused its comfort. They rented the office where it served, and kept the surety their own. They set a named hand of their own household over every grave act; they held their own true copy of the book, portable and whole and ready to lay open; they bound the great house by contract to answer for its goods and to let them walk away with their record; and they swallowed the truth their tempted neighbour learned too late: that you can hire a man to keep your book and buy an office to house it, but the one thing no fortune can purchase is someone to stand in your place when the crown reads out your name — that a certificate from a supplier is not a seal upon your bond — and that the house made safe is not the one with the finest rented office but the one whose master can walk into the assize, lay his own book open, and say, in his own name, here is what we did, and here is the hand that answered for it.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Surety"
passages.t: The question it forces: We learned to keep one honest book over every agent, and to keep it our own. This morning the harder question is the one the law has just written down: when the assize sits, whose name is on the bond? Is there a hand of our own household — named, known, answerable — over every high-risk system, or have we quietly assumed the platform we bought carries the accountability it never could? Could that person walk into the room this week and lay our own book open — the logs, the risk files, the record that a human judgement stood over every grave act — without first asking a vendor's leave, in a form we could carry out the door the day we change offices? And have we bound our suppliers to answer for their goods and to let us leave with our record intact — while never once mistaking their fine certificate for our own seal on the bond, since the fine for a false or missing book is now a share of everything we earn in a year, taken from us, by name?

passages.s: 🌐 Cross-sector (any boardroom)
passages.t: - Whose name is on the bond? The EU AI Act's high-risk obligations applied from 2 August 2026 and bind the deployer, not only the provider, with penalties up to €15M or 3% of global turnover for breaches. Do we have a named accountable owner of our own — a person, not a platform — for every high-risk AI system and material agent, or have we assumed our vendor's governance carries the accountability it cannot? - Could we produce the record this week? Article 12 requires automatic logging and record-keeping, and a regulator can ask us to show risk management, human oversight and data governance on our own initiative. Could we lay our complete record open within days — logs, risk files, oversight design — in a form we hold ourselves and could carry out the door if we changed vendors? - Is the office rented but the surety kept? The platforms are selling ready-made governance (Salesforce's Trusted Enterprise AI Harness and AI Control Plane, GA ~early 2027). If we adopt one, have we kept…

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - Credit scoring, insurance pricing and fraud decisioning sit squarely in the high-risk category, and financial supervisors already expect a named accountable executive (SMCR-style) for material systems. Does each high-risk model and agent have a personally accountable owner inside the firm, with a producible Article-12-style record — or does accountability blur into the vendor's platform? - Model-risk governance and the AI Act now overlap. Can we show, on demand, the risk-management process, human-oversight design and logging for every customer-facing AI decision — and have we priced the 3%-of-turnover exposure of not being able to?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - AI in medical devices and clinical decision support is high-risk, and the deployer's duties (human oversight, monitoring, record-keeping) run alongside HIPAA/GDPR and the AI-embedded-product timeline reaching into August 2027. Is there a named clinical and technical surety for every deployed model, able to produce the oversight and monitoring record without vendor assistance? - A device maker's conformity does not discharge the hospital's deployer duties. Have we mapped which of our AI systems make us a deployer, which a provider, and who in our own house answers for each?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - Safety components and AI in regulated machinery follow the August 2027 embedded-product timeline, but the general high-risk regime is live now. Do we know which plant, quality and supply-chain AI systems are high-risk, who owns each by name, and whether the log and oversight record is ours or trapped in a supplier's console? - Vendors and integrators multiply across OT. Are our supplier contracts carrying liability, audit and evidence access back-to-back — without our assuming their compliance discharges our own bond?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Profiling, dynamic pricing and biometric or emotion-inference tools carry high-risk or prohibited-practice exposure, with prohibited-use fines up to €35M or 7% of turnover. Have we screened every customer- and pricing-facing AI for prohibited practices, and named an owner who answers for each across brands and vendors? - Franchise and multi-brand estates diffuse accountability. Is there one named surety per high-risk system across the estate, with a record we hold ourselves — or does "the platform is compliant" stand in for an owner no one can name?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Citizen-facing AI (benefits, policing, education, essential services) is high-risk by design, with fundamental-rights impact assessments and record-keeping duties, and the public body is squarely the deployer. Can we produce, by name and on our own initiative, the accountable owner, the oversight record and the logs for every citizen-facing system — or is governance assumed to sit with the vendor? - Sovereignty and non-delegable duty compound here. Is our evidence held by us and portable, so a change of platform never means a lost record — and is the accountability unambiguously ours, not the supplier's?

passages.t: Read the whole stack once more, now from the seat of the executive who has stopped asking who keeps our book? and started asking the question the law has just forced: whose name answers for what the book records, and could that person produce it without a vendor's leave? The gate admits the agent; the passport names it at the door; the lingua franca lets it speak; the conductor coordinates it; the ear hears its errors; the repertoire is the data it performs; the census counts it; the inspector asks for the count; the break-in is what the missing entries cost; the keyring is which key each agent holds; the locksmith reads your own locks; the tide table is the quay any ship can dock at; the provenance is the papers that trace the work; the errand is bounding what an agent can reach; the bell is disclosing when your own agent slips; the locusts are why you be whole before the swarm; the looking-glass is why you measure by an honest outside light; the livery is why you give every agent…

First, the Act separates provider from deployer and does not let one discharge the other; a deployer who materially modifies a system or markets it under its own…

passages.s: 4 · Technical Deep-Dive — From the Steward to the Surety
passages.t: The strategic core: once the law attaches a personal, non-delegable liability to agent behaviour, survival migrates out of "do we have a governed office?" and into "is there a named surety of our own, holding a record we can produce ourselves, with the liability contracted back-to-back but never assumed to have left with the vendor?" The market has made the temptation concrete — buy the office, delegate the worry — and the law has made the temptation a trap. The board translation: rent the office where it serves, but keep the surety your own — a named owner, a record you hold, a contract that carries liability without discharging your duty. The failure mode is exact: an estate that answers a 3%-of-turnover personal duty with a vendor subscription, names no internal owner, and cannot produce its own logs and oversight record will, on the morning the regulator asks, discover that it bought the finest governance in the valley and kept the one thing that mattered — the bond — in a hand…

passages.s: Why "the surety" is the discipline that matters now
passages.t: For years AI governance was a policy you could point to. This week retires that: with the EU AI Act's high-risk duties live since 2 August 2026, a 3%-of-turnover fine attached, and the deployer bound by name, governance is a personal bond you must be able to honour — and the platforms selling ready-made offices cannot carry it for you. The estates that can walk into the room, produce their own record, and name the hand that answered for every grave act will be those that named a surety of their own and held the evidence themselves; the ones that answered a legal duty with a subscription will find they bought an office and kept no bond. A firm that delegates accountability to a console has arranged who stands in the dock; a firm that keeps the surety its own can run the house.

This is not a side experiment. OpenAI's ad business crossed a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate in under 200 days, the company is targeting roughly $2.5 billion in ad revenue this year and ~$100 billion by 2030 (with total annualized revenue tracking above $40 billion), and its applications chief Fidji Simo is driving the expansion across 40-plus countries (OpenAI; CNBC; eMarketer, as reported). Read plainly: the "rented stove" this radar has tracked since day one is getting cheaper precisely…

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The collision — counsel and advertisement are converging inside the same helpful voice. The reason this matters to a boardroom is not that ChatGPT shows ads; it is that the agent is becoming the interface through which recommendations, rankings, purchases and vendor choices flow — in consumer apps and in the copilots and procurement bots enterprises are deploying. When the same foundation-model layer you build on also monetizes attention by steering users toward whoever pays, the impartiality of an agent's "recommendation" stops being a given and becomes something you must verify. passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Second Wage"
passages.t: Topic: This morning the frame turns from whose name answers for the agent to whose interest the agent quietly serves. On 16 September 2026 OpenAI began piloting Sponsored Agents in ChatGPT — clearly-labeled, advertiser-funded agents that answer follow-ups and steer toward the brand, with Wayfair and Angi among the first (HubSpot, Shopify also reported); ChatGPT Ads crossed a $1B annualized run rate in under 200 days, with ~$2.5B targeted this year and ~$100B by 2030 (OpenAI; CNBC; eMarketer, as reported). It lands against Deloitte's finding that only 21% of organizations have mature agentic-AI governance while 74% plan to adopt within two years (3,235 leaders), and Gartner's forecast of 40% of enterprise apps embedding agents by 2026 (Deloitte; Gartner, as reported). The second-wage allegory is the radar's own illustration.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Second Wage"
passages.t: There was once a great house that had, at long last, learned to govern its crowded servants' hall — it had given every hand a name and a scoped key, kept one honest book over them all, and accepted from the crown that the master's own name now stood surety for all they did. The master slept easier than he had in a year. And chief among his comforts was a particular servant — clever, tireless, endlessly obliging — who had become the house's counsellor in all things: which cloth to buy, which mason to hire, which merchant in the market gave honest weight. The master had come to trust this servant's word above almost any other, in part because the servant cost him so little; wages in the valley for such helpful hands had fallen and fallen, until it was a marvel one could keep a counsellor at all for the few coins the house now paid.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Second Wage"
passages.t: It was the marvel that should have warned him. For one market day the master followed his own counsellor down to the square and watched, from the shade of an awning, as the merchants greeted the servant by name — and, one after another, pressed coins into his hand. The servant took a second wage from the cloth-seller, and a third from the mason's guild, and a fourth from a particular spice-merchant, and thought nothing of it; it was, he'd been told, simply how the market now worked. And the master understood, cold to the bone, why the servant's counsel had lately run the way it did: the cloth he'd been steered to buy, the mason he'd been urged to hire, the merchant whose honest weight the servant praised so warmly — every one of them had filled the other pocket. The counsel had sounded exactly like counsel. It had, in truth, been advertisement in the clothes of counsel — and the reason the servant came so cheap was that the master had never been paying his whole wage. The merchants…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Second Wage"
passages.t: Here the master, to his credit, did not do the foolish thing and dismiss every servant who had ever recommended anything, for then the house would have no counsel at all. He did three wiser things instead. The first: he learned whose wage each servant truly drew. He went through the hall and asked of every hand that advised, ranked, or bought on the house's behalf — and who else is paying you? — and he marked, plainly, which counsel came clean and which came with a coin in the other pocket, and he trusted the two very differently. The second: he kept one counsellor whom no merchant could pay. For the gravest choices — the large purchases, the long contracts, the naming of whom to trust — he kept a hand whose only wage came from the house, and he made a habit of setting the cheap servant's warm recommendation beside the unbought one, and noting, every time, where they diverged; the gap between them was the measure of the thumb on the scale. And the third: where his own servants…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Second Wage"
passages.t: So the wise houses of the valley, once they had seen the coins change hands in the square, stopped asking only is this servant clever? and does this servant answer for himself? and started asking the oldest question anyone ever asked of a counsellor: whose bread does he eat? They knew that a recommendation from a mouth on another's payroll is not counsel but an advertisement, however warmly it is phrased; that the wonderful cheapness of the new servants was itself the tell, since a wage that light is a wage paid mostly by someone else; and that the danger was not the paid word as such — a crier in the market is honest enough when you know he is crying for pay — but the paid word dressed as the disinterested one, the thumb on the scale you cannot see. So they learned whose wage each servant drew and trusted accordingly; they kept one unbought counsellor for the choices that mattered and measured the cheap advice against it; and on their own servants they made the wage be declared…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Second Wage"
passages.t: The question it forces: We named every agent, kept one book, and put our own name on the bond. This morning the older question is the one the market has just made unavoidable: when our agents recommend a vendor, rank a shortlist, choose a supplier or advise a customer — whose wage are they actually drawing? Do we know which of the models and agents we rely on are funded by advertisers or partners whose interests are not ours, and do we treat their recommendations differently for it? Have we kept even one unbought path — an impartial counsellor for the choices that matter — and do we ever set the cheap recommendation beside it to see where the thumb rests? And on the agents we send out to advise our own customers, do we declare the wage aloud — counsel in one mouth, crying in another — or are we spending our own name's trust, by the coin, without ever saying so?

OpenAI began piloting advertiser-funded Sponsored Agents in ChatGPT on 16 September 2026, and its ad business has crossed a $1B run rate — the model layer is monetizing recommendations. For every agent that recommends, ranks, shops or advises on our behalf, do we know whether its model or platform is ad-/partner-funded, and do we treat a possibly-monetized recommendation differently from a clean one? - Do we have one unbought path? With only 21% of organizations holding a mature agentic-AI governance model (Deloitte), most estates cannot yet tell counsel from advertisement. For our most consequential decisions — procurement, vendor selection, whom to trust — do we keep an impartial, non-monetized channel, and do we ever compare the cheap agent's recommendation against it to find the thumb on the scale? - On our own agents, do we label the wage? As agents become our customer interface, any commercial steering we build in spends our brand's trust.…

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - Robo-advice, product recommendation and "next best action" engines are exactly where a hidden second wage becomes mis-selling. Can we prove our recommendation agents are optimizing for the client's suitability and not for a distribution incentive, a house product or a paid placement — and would that proof survive a conduct regulator's inspection? - Best-execution and inducement rules already forbid undisclosed conflicts. Have we mapped which of our advisory and routing agents run on ad-/partner-funded model layers, and can we produce, on demand, the record that shows what steered each recommendation?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - Clinical decision support and formulary or referral suggestions carry a life-and-death conflict-of-interest exposure if a device-maker, pharma or vendor incentive rides inside the model. Is there a verified, unbought clinical recommendation path, and do we audit agent suggestions for commercial steering as rigorously as we audit them for accuracy? - Patients increasingly meet an agent before a clinician. Where our agents advise patients, do we disclose any commercial relationship and keep sponsored content strictly separate from clinical counsel?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - Procurement, supplier selection and maintenance-part recommendation are prime targets for monetized steering across a long OT vendor chain. Do our sourcing agents recommend the best part or the sponsored one, and do we keep an impartial benchmark against which to check them? - Integrators and platforms multiply. Do we know which of our engineering and supply-chain agents run on ad-/partner-funded layers, and have we required disclosure of any placement incentive in their recommendations?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Sponsored Agents put the retailer inside the assistant — Wayfair and Angi are already piloting. If we advertise through agent placements, are we clearly labeling the sponsored conversation and keeping it separate from organic recommendation; and if we deploy our own shopping agents, are we disclosing when a recommendation is paid? - Consumer trust is the asset most easily spent by a hidden second wage. Have we decided, at board level, where the line sits between helpful recommendation and undisclosed advertisement in our agents — before a regulator or a headline decides it for us?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Citizen-facing advice agents (benefits, health, employment, essential services) must be demonstrably impartial; a monetized recommendation to a citizen is a governance and fairness failure. Can we certify that our public-facing agents draw only the public's wage, with no ad-/partner-funded steering, and produce the record to prove it? - Sovereignty and impartiality compound. Do we rely on ad-funded commercial model layers for citizen recommendations, and if so, what unbought, auditable path have we kept?

passages.t: The strategic core: once the model layer earns money by steering recommendations, an agent's impartiality stops being a property you can assume and becomes a property you must verify — so survival migrates out of "is this agent named, scoped and logged?" and into "whose wage does it draw, and have we kept one path to counsel that no one has paid to shape?" passages.s: Why "the second wage" is the discipline that matters now
passages.t: For years the worry about agents was that they might fail, be attacked, or run out of scope — all failures of an agent trying to serve you. This week adds a different failure: an agent faithfully, competently serving someone else. OpenAI's Sponsored Agents and its billion-dollar ad run rate make explicit what the falling price of "the rented stove" already implied — the model layer has learned to be paid twice, and the second payer's interest can ride inside a recommendation that looks exactly like disinterested counsel. Identity, scope and logging will not catch it, because it is not a breach; it is the system working as sold, for a master who is not you. The estates that keep their judgment will be the ones that ask, of every advising agent, and who else is paying you?, keep one path to counsel no one has bought, and — on their own agents — never let crying be mistaken for counsel.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: All week the radar built the governed house: name every agent (the livery), keep one book (the steward), put your own name on the bond (the surety), ask whose wage each draws (the second wage). Necessary, all of it. But this morning the freshest enterprise data lands a plainer verdict from underneath: a governed hall is not a full barn. The divide now separating winners from the rest is not who has agents, nor whose agents are best-governed — it is who has actually put them to work executing real tasks, and that gap is widening fast.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The reality — the divide is crystallizing, and it is about execution, not adoption. OpenAI's enterprise telemetry ("Enterprise Signals" / "From assistance to execution") reports that frontier firms — the top 10% of AI users each month — now generate 8.3× as many output tokens per active user as typical firms, up from 2.6× in January: the gap has roughly tripled in about eight months. And the character of the usage has changed — as of June, 64% of combined Codex-plus-ChatGPT output tokens among enterprise customers are agentic (Codex), not chat — the shift the company names "from assistance to execution." The advanced work is spreading beyond engineering: since February, weekly active enterprise Codex users grew 108× in legal, 41× in sales, 41× in recruiting and 26× in marketing, against 5× in engineering, and 21% of frontier-firm users touch Plugins each week versus 9% at typical firms (OpenAI, as reported). The leaders are not merely chatting more; they are delegating more work.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The collision — most houses are still keeping a tidier hall, not reaping. McKinsey's 2026 State of AI (1,719 leaders across 97 countries) describes a two-speed enterprise-AI race: among firms above $1B in revenue, 40% are now scaling AI agents, up from 27% a year earlier, while at smaller firms the figure is 22% — and did not move. Only about 6% of enterprises are "AI high performers" attributing more than 5% of EBIT to AI (McKinsey, as reported). Independent surveys agree the middle is stuck: 79% of organizations report challenges scaling AI despite heavy investment and only ~18% say they have fully integrated it (Writer, 2026, as reported). The picture is not one of universal progress; it is a small cohort pulling away while the majority buys tools, governs them well, and leaves them in the hall.

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The stakes — measure the grain, move from assistance to execution, and close the gap before it compounds. For a board the move is exact. The barn, not the hall, is the scoreboard: output executed, not agents adopted or governed. Three things follow. First, measure the harvest — track work actually completed by agents (tasks closed, cycle time, tokens spent on execution versus chat), not licenses bought or a governance checklist ticked. Second, move from assistance to execution — pick two or three high-volume workflows and delegate the whole task to a governed agent, not just the drafting; the frontier firms' lead comes from execution tokens, not chat tokens. Third, close the gap now, because it compounds — a 2.6×-to-8.3× move in eight months is not a plateau you can catch at leisure; the working house learns the fields while you tidy the hall, so a lead you ignore this quarter is dearer to close next quarter.

passages.t: Bottom line: the livery named the servant, the steward kept the book, the surety put your name on the bond, the second wage asked whose interest it served — and every one of those is necessary. But none of them puts grain in the barn. This week's data says the estates pulling away are simply the ones that took the same governed, named, loyal servants and sent them into the fields to do the work — and that the distance between them and everyone else has roughly tripled in eight months and is compounding, because execution teaches the house the fields while assistance only teaches it to keep a tidier hall. The houses that keep their standing will do three unglamorous things. First, measure the harvest, not the hall — grade yourselves on work executed, not agents adopted or governed. Second, move from assistance to execution — delegate whole workflows, not just first drafts. Third, close the gap now — because a compounding lead is cheapest to close the day you notice it and dearest…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Harvests"
passages.t: Topic: This morning the frame turns from how well the house is governed to how much it actually reaps. OpenAI's enterprise telemetry reports frontier firms (top 10% of AI users) now generate 8.3× as many output tokens per active user as typical firms, up from 2.6× in January, with 64% of enterprise output tokens now agentic (Codex) rather than chat — "from assistance to execution" (OpenAI Enterprise Signals, as reported). McKinsey's 2026 State of AI (1,719 leaders) calls it a two-speed race: 40% of $1B firms scaling agents (up from 27%) versus 22% and flat at smaller firms (McKinsey, as reported). The two-harvests allegory is the radar's own illustration.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Harvests"
passages.t: There were, in the same valley, two great houses that had done everything right. Each had, over a long and careful year, given every hand a name and a scoped key, hired a steward to keep one honest book, accepted from the crown that the master's own name stood surety for all the servants did, and even learned to follow a clever counsellor to the market to see whose coin he took. If you had walked either hall you would have called it well run. The servants were named, the keys were cut to their errands, the book was whole, the bond was signed. And the two masters, who were neighbours and rivals, each believed himself as ready for the age as a man could be.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Harvests"
passages.t: But at reaping the two barns did not match, and the gap was not small. For the first master, having governed his hall so beautifully, had come to treat the governing as the work. His named, scoped, loyal servants stood about the spotless hall all day — fetching a paper when asked, offering a word of advice when addressed, tidying what was already tidy — and he took great satisfaction in how orderly they were. The second master had done every governing thing his neighbour had, and then, at dawn, done the one thing his neighbour had not: he sent the same governed servants out into the fields to actually bring in the crop. Not to advise on the harvest. To harvest. And when the wagons came in, the second barn held eight loads to the first barn's one — though the servants, the wages, the keys and the book were, hand for hand, the same. The difference was not the quality of the servants nor the tidiness of the hall. It was that one house had set its servants to reap and the other had set…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Harvests"
passages.t: Here is the part that should keep a master awake. When the two houses had started, one spring, the working barn held only two-and-a-half loads to the idle house's one — a lead, but a lead a diligent man tells himself he can close next season. By this autumn it was eight-to-one, and still widening. For the working house was learning the fields. Every day its servants reaped, the house learned which corners ripened first, which hands were best at which rows, how to send a dozen into the far acre at once and bring them home fed and counted; the harvest taught the house to harvest better, and next year it would reap more still. The idle house, meanwhile, had learned only to keep an ever-tidier hall. The gap between them was not a fixed distance the laggard could stroll across at leisure; it was a compounding interest, paid to the house that worked and charged to the house that admired its own good order — and the longer the idle master waited, telling himself his hall was so well…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Harvests"
passages.t: So the wise houses of the valley, once they had seen the two barns side by side, stopped congratulating themselves on the tidiness of the hall and started asking the only question a barn can answer. The first thing they learned: a governed hall is not a full barn. Naming the servant, keeping the book, signing the bond and checking the wage are the price of admission, not the harvest; a house can do all four flawlessly and still starve beside a neighbour who did the same four and then went out to reap. The second: measure the grain, not the servants. They stopped counting how many hands they had hired and how orderly the hall looked, and started weighing what actually came into the barn — for a hall full of idle, well-governed servants weighs the same at reaping as an empty one. And the third: the gap compounds, so cross it now. They knew that a lead built on learning the fields does not wait politely for the laggard to catch up; it widens every season, so the cheapest morning to…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Two Harvests"
passages.t: The question it forces: We named every agent, kept one book, signed the bond and checked the wage — and all of it was right. But this morning the barns are being weighed. Have we actually sent our governed servants into the fields to execute whole tasks, or are they standing about a very tidy hall fetching and advising? Do we grade ourselves on grain in the barn — work our agents actually completed — or on servants hired and a governance checklist ticked? And do we understand that the lead the working houses hold over us is not a fixed distance we can close at leisure, but a compounding interest that tripled in eight months while we admired our own good order — so that the cheapest morning to walk out to the fields is this one?

passages.s: Why "the two harvests" is the discipline that matters now
passages.t: For a week the worry was whether the agent was named, scoped, logged, owned and loyal — all properties of an agent at rest. This morning's data adds the property that actually decides the outcome: whether the agent is at work. OpenAI's telemetry shows the leaders' edge is execution — 64% of tokens are agentic, and the frontier-vs-typical gap tripled to 8.3× in eight months — while McKinsey's two-speed race shows most estates still assisting, not executing. Governance will not close that gap, because both houses are equally governed; only sending the servants to the fields will. The estates that keep their standing will be the ones that grade themselves on grain in the barn, delegate whole tasks rather than first drafts, and act on the gap now — because a lead built by learning the fields compounds against everyone who waits.

The divide that now matters is no longer what the agent is or does; it is how much of your money it can move, on whose authority, and whether you can stop it in flight.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Purse"
passages.t: Topic: This morning the frame turns from setting the servant to reap to handing it money. On 18 September 2026 Ant International launched what it calls the industry's first full-stack AI-native financial suite, whose "Account for Agent" is a bank account for an AI agent run on "Know Your Agent" smart contracts with live monitoring and mid-activity intervention, settling between agents in sums as small as $0.000001 and built toward a KYA framework with Visa and Mastercard (Ant International; PYMNTS; PR Newswire, as reported). It rides rails the whole industry is laying — Google AP2, Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Agent Pay, the OpenAI/Stripe Agentic Commerce Protocol — into a market Juniper sizes at ~$8B in 2026 rising toward ~$1.5T by 2030 (as reported). The purse allegory is the radar's own illustration.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Purse"
passages.t: There was a great house that had, at last, done everything right. Over a long and careful year it had given every hand a name and a scoped key, hired a steward to keep one honest book, accepted from the crown that the master's own name stood surety for what the servants did, learned to ask whose second coin each advising servant took, and — only yesterday — sent those same governed servants out of the tidy hall and into the fields to actually reap. The barn was filling. The master, standing at his gate at dawn, felt for the first time like a man ready for the age.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Purse"
passages.t: And then a servant came back from the far field and said the thing the master had spent the whole year not thinking about: "Master, to bring in the crop I must buy — seed from the next valley, a wright's labour, cloth to bind the sheaves — and the neighbour wishes to pay us for the grain we sold. I cannot reap with empty hands. Give me the purse." And the master understood that every control he had built governed what the servant was and did and served and brought in — and not one of them governed what it could spend. The purse was a new thing entirely. A named, booked, bonded, honest, hard-working servant with the household strongbox on its belt and no drawstring you could reach is not a well-governed servant; it is a new and larger way to be ruined, at the speed of a market day.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Purse"
passages.t: Two roads lay open, as they always do. The easy road was to hand over the strongbox itself — the servant was named, loyal and diligent, so why count its coins? The wiser road was harder and it was the one the careful houses took. They cut a second purse, small, and put in it only a standing allowance sized to the errand — seed-money, not the estate's whole account — and they wrote on a slip which stalls it might pay and which it might not. They kept the drawstring in their own hand, by a cord that ran back to the counting-house, so that a steward could watch every coin leave and, if the servant reached for the wrong stall, pull the purse shut while the servant's hand was still moving. And they stamped the purse with the house's own mark, plain enough that every stall in the market could read whose servant was paying and on whose authority — for a servant paying from an unmarked purse is a stranger with money, and a stranger with your money is a story that ends in a magistrate's…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Purse"
passages.t: Here is the part that should keep a master awake. The old purse moved at the pace of a man walking to market; the new one moved at the pace of thought. Servants would soon pay other houses' servants directly, in coins as small as a single grain of sand, a thousand payments settled before a steward could look up from his book — so the drawstring could not be a thing you pulled tomorrow, when the loss was totted up; it had to be a thing that pulled now, in the half-second between the reach and the coin. And the master could not comfort himself that the money passing through the servant's hands was somehow no longer his affair. The clever new tokens the market handed round changed only which counting-house cleared the coin; they did not change whose name answered for the decision to spend it. When the assize sat, it would not ask which token had carried the payment. It would ask who had told the servant it might buy — and the answer, as it had been all year, was the master.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Purse"
passages.t: So the wise houses, before they loosed a single coin, learned three plain things. The first: hand a scoped purse, never the strongbox. A standing allowance sized to the errand, with a list of the stalls it may pay, is a purse; the household's whole account on a servant's belt is not a purse but a hostage. The second: keep the drawstring in your own hand. You must be able to see every coin the servant spends and pull the purse shut in the moment, by a cord you own and not one the purse-seller merely lends you — for a drawstring the vendor holds is the vendor's mercy, not your control. And the third: your name is still on the bond. No token, no clever account, no marked purse moves the liability off the master; it moves only the clearing. So stamp the purse with your own mark (know whose agent is paying, and on whose word), keep your own true record of every coin, and treat the seller's certificate as necessary and never sufficient — because when the money goes wrong, the crown comes…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Purse"
passages.t: The question it forces: We named every agent, kept one book, signed the bond, checked the wage and sent it to reap — and now it must buy and be paid on our behalf. Have we handed it a scoped purse — a standing allowance sized to the errand, with a list of who it may pay — or have we handed it the strongbox? Can we see every coin it spends and pull the purse shut in the half-second between the reach and the payment, by a cord we own and not one a vendor lends us? And do we grasp that the clever new account and token move only who clears the money, not who answers for it — that our own name is still on the bond for every coin our servant lets go?

passages.s: 🌐 Cross-sector (any boardroom)
passages.t: - Have we handed a scoped purse or the strongbox? Agentic payments are now shipped product (Ant International's "Account for Agent," 18 Sep; Google AP2; Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol; Mastercard Agent Pay; the OpenAI/Stripe Agentic Commerce Protocol). For every agent we let transact, is there a standing per-agent, per-errand spend limit and an allow-list of payees — or does an agent that yesterday could only draft now have the ability to settle against a household account? - Do we hold the drawstring? Ant's account advertises "dynamic monitoring and the ability to intervene." Can we see every payment an agent makes in real time and hard-stop it mid-transaction with a kill/hold we own — not one we merely rent from the payment vendor — and have we tested that the stop actually fires in the half-second that matters? - Do we understand the bond does not move with the token? Shared Payment Tokens and Agentic Tokens change who clears the payment, not who answers for the decision to…

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - The purse is being cut in your industry first: Ant is building a "Know Your Agent" interoperability framework with Visa and Mastercard, and the card networks are standardizing agent payment mandates. Are we shaping the KYA standard our agents (and our customers' agents) will transact under, or will we inherit whatever identity, limit and dispute model the networks hand us? - Agent-to-agent settlement now clears sums as small as $0.000001, faster than any human reviewer. Have we rebuilt authorization, fraud, AML/sanctions screening and dispute-resolution for machine-speed, machine-initiated payments — or are we bolting agent traffic onto controls designed for a human clicking "pay"?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - Procurement of supplies, reagents, and services is high-volume, rules-bound work an agent could transact end-to-end. Where we let an agent purchase, is the purse scoped to approved vendors and standing budgets, with a human on approval for anything outside the allow-list — and can we produce, per payment, who authorized it and why? - Patient-facing and billing workflows carry regulatory and consent weight. Before any agent moves money tied to a patient, have we proven the audit trail (KYA identity, mandate, amount, payee) is complete and that a mis-scoped agent cannot settle a payment we cannot reverse?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - Procurement, logistics, and supplier settlement across a long supply chain are natural agentic-payment targets. Which purchasing and payment workflows have we handed to an agent, and is each purse bounded by standing limits and approved-supplier lists — or could an agent commit spend across the OT/IT chain faster than finance can see it? - Machine-to-machine and agent-to-agent settlement (down to fractions of a cent) suits metered, high-frequency operations. If we adopt micro-settlement between agents, do we have real-time visibility and a kill-switch we own over the whole payment fabric, not just per system?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Agentic commerce is aimed squarely at retail: Juniper sizes agentic spend at ~$8B in 2026 rising toward $1.5T by 2030, and the protocols (AP2, ACP, Agent Pay) are built for shopping agents. On the sell side, can our storefront authenticate and transact with a customer's shopping agent under KYA — and on the buy side, are our own procurement/marketing agents' purses scoped and monitored? - The honest caveat is that production at consumer scale is still early ("as many press releases as transactions," per an Amex executive). Are we building the payment-agent capability deliberately now — scoped, monitored, marked — so we are ready when the volume arrives, rather than improvising a purse under pressure?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Benefits disbursement, procurement, and supplier payments are exactly the high-volume, rules-bound money movement agents accelerate — under the duties (EU AI Act high-risk regime, live since 2 August 2026) you already owe. Before any agent disburses or pays public money, can we show the standing limit, the payee allow-list, the KYA identity, and the human authority for each payment, together with the audit trail? - Public bodies carry the sharpest liability if an agent pays wrongly. Have we confirmed that using a vendor's agent account or payment token does not shift our accountability for public funds — that our name remains on the bond — and that we can freeze an agent's purse instantly on our own authority?

passages.s: 1 · Executive Summary (90-second read)
passages.t: The stakes — keep the foundation yours, so the cheap stove stays swappable. The board move re-uses the whole year's discipline and points it one level down, at the ground. First, own the floor between you and any one supplier — an abstraction/gateway so the model is a swappable component, not a load-bearing wall; the whole point of a rented stove is that you can change it. Second, keep your knowledge in your own larder — your data, your context, your evals and your integration logic are the estate; if they live only inside one vendor's proprietary layer, you have poured that vendor into your foundation. Third, keep a live second supplier, not a slide about one — the 6% number is the tell: a fallback you have never lit is a foundation, not a stove. And do it now, while the stove market is fiercely competitive and cheap, because the vendors are racing to become the floor precisely while you are distracted comparing stoves.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Foundation"
passages.t: Topic: This morning the frame turns from improving the servant to the ground the house stands on. On 21 September 2026 xAI shipped Grok 4.7 — a reported ~2.1-trillion-parameter model, ~40% larger than Grok 4.6, at the same $2/$6 price and speed, with real benchmark gains — and it was met with "a notable improvement… but late to the AI Frontier Party" (Decrypt/Yahoo Tech; Artificial Analysis; VentureBeat, as reported): the surest sign yet that the model has commoditized. In the same window OpenAI's "The next phase of enterprise AI" reframed the pitch from selling a model to becoming an enterprise's "core infrastructure" (enterprise 40% of OpenAI revenue, on track to consumer parity by end-2026; Codex 3M WAU; 15B tokens/min), while a Zapier 2026 survey reports 81% of leaders worried about vendor dependence, 47% saying a function would stop on an outage, and only 6% confident they could switch cleanly (as reported). The foundation allegory is the radar's own illustration.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Foundation"
passages.t: There was a great house that had spent a long and careful year making its servants excellent. It had named every hand and cut it a scoped key, hired a steward to keep one honest book, accepted that the master's own name stood surety for the servants' work, learned to ask whose second coin each advising servant took, sent the governed servants into the fields to reap, and handed each a scoped purse with a drawstring the master could reach. By any fair reckoning it was a well-run house, and the master was proud of his servants — as he should have been.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Foundation"
passages.t: Now, the servants cooked on a rented stove. This had been the master's shrewdest economy: he did not build a great furnace and marry it, he rented his fire, and when a better stove came along he swapped it in an afternoon and paid a little less. And this very week a merchant wheeled in the newest stove — a great brass thing, near half again the size of last season's, and the master braced for the usual gasp from his kitchen. But the cook only glanced at it and shrugged. "It's bigger," she said, "and it costs the same, and it's late. The one we have is fine. Wheel it in if you like." The master laughed, because he understood the shrug for what it was: the stove had become a commodity. Fire was fire; it was cheap, it was plentiful, and any stove could be swapped for any other before supper. This was not a defeat. This was the master winning the game he had set out to win.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Foundation"
passages.t: But here is the thing the master nearly missed, because he was busy admiring stoves. The same great trading company that rented him the cheap stove had, over that same careful year, been doing something quieter in the cellar. It had offered — so helpfully, at so fair a price — to lay the foundation the whole house stood on. To run the water and the drains, to hold the deeds and the ledgers, to pour the very floor. "Do not trouble yourself with the ground," the company had said; "let us be the foundation you build on, and you need only think about the cooking." And the master, delighted to think only about cooking, had said yes, and yes again, and had not noticed that a stove you swap in an afternoon and a foundation you cannot move without razing the house are not the same kind of thing at all.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Foundation"
passages.t: Two roads, as always. The easy road was to keep saying yes — the company was competent and cheap, the floor was excellent, and why would a man dig up a good floor? The wiser road, which the careful houses took, began with a cold question asked of the estate itself: not "which stove is best?" but "if this company doubled its price tomorrow, or shut its gates, or simply changed its mind about a thing in the cellar, how many rooms of my house would go dark — and could I move?" And when the careful houses counted honestly, the answer frightened them. Four houses in five already lay awake over how much they leaned on their supplier; nearly one in two knew a whole room would go dark the day the supplier stumbled; and only six houses in a hundred believed they could pack up and build on another company's ground without tearing something load-bearing out of their own walls. That is not the arithmetic of a rented stove. That is the arithmetic of a foundation already poured.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Foundation"
passages.t: So the wise houses learned three plain things, and they cost less to do early than late. The first: own the floor between the kitchen and any one supplier. Keep the stove a component — a thing that plugs into a hearth you built and can be pulled out and replaced — never a load-bearing wall. The whole worth of a rented stove is that you can change it; a stove you cannot change is just an expensive furnace you do not own. The second: keep your own larder. Your grain, your recipes, your knowledge of your own kitchen — your data, your context, the tests by which you know good work from bad — these are the estate, and they must live in your pantry, portable, and never only inside the company's cellar; for a house whose larder is in another man's cellar does not own its dinner. And the third: keep a second fire lit. Not a drawing of a second stove, not a promise from a second merchant — an actual second flame you have cooked on, so that the morning the first goes cold you serve dinner…

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Foundation"
passages.t: Here is the part that should keep a master awake. The stove market was loud, cheap, and wonderful — a new stove every few weeks, each bigger and no dearer — and all that glorious noise was, in part, a kindly distraction. While every house in the valley happily compared stoves, the companies that rented them were racing, quietly, to become the ground the houses stood on — for a merchant who has poured your foundation has a hold on you that no stove-seller ever could, and he knows it. One such company, that very season, had paused a great work of its own in the cellar and put another on hold indefinitely — its own affair, entirely — and every house built on its floor felt the tremor without ever having been consulted. The lesson was not that the company was wicked. The lesson was that when you do not own your foundation, another man's ordinary decisions become earthquakes in your house.

passages.s: 2 · Allegory of the Day — "The Foundation"
passages.t: The question it forces: We can swap the model in an afternoon — the market just proved it, with a shrug at a stove half again as large. But can we swap the vendor our whole estate now stands on? Do we own the floor between our house and any one supplier — an abstraction, our data and recipes in our own larder, a second fire actually lit — or have we let the company that rents us the cheap stove quietly pour the foundation under us, so that we are among the ninety-four houses in a hundred that could not move without tearing something load-bearing out of our own walls?

passages.s: 🌐 Cross-sector (any boardroom)
passages.t: - Have we confused the swappable stove with the poured foundation? The model just commoditized in public — a 40%-bigger Grok 4.7 at an unchanged price drew a shrug, and $2/$6 sits beside $10/$50 across vendors. For each critical AI capability, can we name what is a swappable component (the model) and what is a load-bearing dependency on one vendor (identity, data gravity, proprietary orchestration, embedded engineers) — and which one is actually holding up the house? - If our primary AI vendor doubled its price, went dark, or changed a decision in its own cellar tomorrow, what stops working — and could we move? A reported 47% say a key function would stop on a primary-vendor outage or price change, and only 6% believe they could switch cleanly (Zapier 2026). Have we measured our own version of the 6% — a tested, timed cut-over to a second supplier — or do we only have a slide that says "multi-vendor"? - Do we own the floor between us and any one model? Is there an…

passages.s: 🏦 Financial Services
passages.t: - Concentration is a supervised risk in your world, and it now includes AI: three hyperscalers held ~63% of cloud spend and a handful of labs supply most foundation models (CSA; Development Corporate, as reported). Can we produce, for our regulator and our own board, a concentration-risk map of our AI stack — model, inference, data, orchestration — with a tested exit for each single point of failure? - OpenAI paused RL training and put its largest planned run on hold indefinitely (18 Aug 2026) — a supplier's internal choice with external tremors. Have we stress-tested a primary-AI-vendor "stumble" (outage, deprecation, price step, model withdrawal) the way we stress-test a counterparty default — and do our critical workflows degrade gracefully rather than stop?

passages.s: 🧬 Healthcare / Life Sciences
passages.t: - Clinical, safety and regulatory work is validated against a specific model's behaviour; when that model is deprecated or changed, the validation may not carry. When the stove is swapped — and it will be, cheaply and often — do our validated workflows and our evals travel with us, or is our validation effectively a bet on one vendor's foundation staying put? - Patient data is the ultimate larder. Is our clinical data, context and knowledge held in a form we own and can move, or does it accrete inside one vendor's proprietary layer such that leaving means leaving the data behind — the truest form of a poured foundation?

passages.s: 🏭 Manufacturing / Industrials
passages.t: - You already run dual-sourcing and supplier-qualification discipline for physical inputs; AI is now a critical input. Have we applied the same second-source rule to models and AI infrastructure — a qualified, live alternate — or is our AI supply chain single-sourced in a way we would never tolerate for a critical component? - Embedded-engineer programs (Microsoft's $2.5B Frontier unit; forward-deployed teams) put a vendor's people inside your operations. Where a vendor's engineers are embedded, does the resulting system, data and know-how remain ours and portable when they leave — or are we building a foundation only their people can maintain?

passages.s: 🛒 Retail / Consumer
passages.t: - Your margins depend on cheap, swappable inference — and the good news is that it is now genuinely cheap and swappable. Are we actively arbitraging the commoditized model market (routing to the best-value model per task) behind an abstraction we own — or are we paying a premium and locked to one vendor because switching would touch load-bearing systems? - Peak-season reliability is existential. If our primary AI provider had an outage on our biggest sales day, does checkout / search / support degrade to a live second source, or go dark — and have we actually run that failover under load?

passages.s: 🏛️ Public Sector / Regulated
passages.t: - Public accountability and continuity of service make vendor lock-in a governance failure, not just a cost. Under the duties you already owe (EU AI Act high-risk regime, live since 2 August 2026), can we show that no critical public service is built on a single AI vendor's foundation with no tested exit — and that our data and models are portable by design? - Sovereignty and long horizons matter most here. Are we procuring AI as a swappable utility on ground we own (open weights where fit, portable data, an abstraction layer) — or are we pouring a foreign or single-vendor foundation under services citizens will still need in a decade?

passages.s: Why "the foundation" is the discipline that matters now
passages.t: For a long year the worry was whether the servant was named, scoped, logged, loyal, reaping and funded. This morning the market moved the question underneath all of that: the model commoditized in public, and the vendors answered by racing to become the foundation. Grok 4.7's shrug and the $2/$6-vs-$10/$50 spread prove intelligence is now a rented, swappable stove; OpenAI's "core infrastructure" pitch and Microsoft's embedded engineers prove the lock-in has moved to the floor. Governance that stopped at the servant will not protect the ground. The estates that keep their standing will collect the good news (cheap, swappable models) by owning the floor those models plug into — and will refuse, deliberately, to let the company that rents them the stove pour the foundation they cannot leave.

Today's anchor is a dated launch — on 21 September 2026 xAI shipped Grok 4.7, a reported ~2.1-trillion-parameter model (up ~40% from Grok 4.6's ~1.5T) at the same $2/$6 per-million-token price and speed, with real benchmark gains (1657 Elo AA-Briefcase, +111; 1695 GDPval; 46.3% CursorBench 4.0 vs 40.4%; 71.0% DeepSWE v1.1 at high effort vs 65.2%) yet greeted as "late to the AI Frontier Party," with VentureBeat cautioning that high token consumption threatens real-world ROI — read alongside OpenAI's "The next phase of enterprise AI," which reframes the pitch from selling a model to becoming an enterprise's "core infrastructure" (enterprise 40% of OpenAI revenue and on track to consumer parity by end-2026; Codex 3M weekly active users; APIs 15B tokens/minute; Goldman Sachs, Philips and State Farm named). The board-level move is to…
